en: The Mañjuśrī-parinirmita-samādhi Sūtra, Scroll One,
also titled the Ajātaśatru-rāja-parivarta,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: On the True Beings (Part One) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering thirty-two thousand, and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.

All were noble sages who understood everything without exception; these great beings and mahāsattvas had fully mastered their supernormal powers, attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, and realized the patience of non-attachment and the non-arising of phenomena. They thoroughly comprehended meditative practices and perceived the minds of sentient beings, preaching the Dharma to each according to what was necessary for their deliverance.

The gods of the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā Sahāmpati, along with countless other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, each with hundreds of thousands of followers, all came together for the assembly.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was on a beam in a different location on one side of the mountain, together with twenty-five virtuous men, expounding and discussing the Dharma.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Dragon Head,
Bodhisattva Dragon Bestower, Bodhisattva Endowed with Head, Bodhisattva Treasury of Head, Bodhisattva Lotus Head,
Bodhisattva Lotus Treasury of Head, Bodhisattva Sustainer of Beings, and Bodhisattva Sustainer of the Earth.
...Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, Bodhisattva Siṃhamati,
Bodhisattva Siṃhakramagarjitasvara, Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Bodhisattva Citta-utpādadharmacakrapravartin,
Bodhisattva Sarvavākpathanirukti, Bodhisattva Vāgīśa, Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi, and Bodhisattva Mahāparvata.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, the Bodhisattva Priyarāja, the Bodhisattva Anantavīkṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Anantadharmapracāra,
the Bodhisattva Māradarśanātikrānta, the Bodhisattva Aśoka-pradāna, and the Bodhisattva Sarvaparipṛcchā-vyākaraṇa—
these are the twenty-five noble beings (satpuruṣa).
In the Tuṣita Heaven there were four devaputras who together attended upon the Youth Mañjuśrī.
Their names were:
the Devaputra Samantakusuma, the Devaputra Prabhākusuma, the Devaputra Surabhi, and the Devaputra Dharmacaryānupravṛtta.
Furthermore, there were other sons of heaven, beyond counting, who all came to attend upon him.
Such upright men and these sons of heaven likewise sat together in assembly, each engaging in discourse. This group addressed one another, saying:

"Virtuous ones, do you wish to know that the Buddha’s wisdom is vast and universal, limitless, inconceivable, and immeasurable? There is no one capable of exhausting its ultimate bounds through final liberation. One cannot fathom this great virtue and armor with a limited mind; by what skillful means should one vow to don the armor of moral virtue so as to attain this Great Vehicle, the Buddha-vehicle, the vehicle of universal omniscience, and the inconceivable vehicle—is this how one should follow the Way?"
The Bodhisattva Nāgaśīrṣa said:

"To accumulate merit without ever becoming weary or satisfied, to establish immeasurable blessings and prosperity, and yet not to lose the armor of virtuous precepts—acting in all things without expectation—is to correspond with the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna."
The Bodhisattva Nāgadatta said:

"One who universally expands an impartial mind to harmonize their will, warms and moistens their nature to soften their intent, and whose heart is benevolent and profound as they firmly abide in right vows—donning the armor of preceptual virtue for the sake of all supernormal wisdoms and liberating others from birth and death—such a person corresponds to the Mahāyāna and its various supernormal wisdoms!"
The Bodhisattva Śīlagupta said:

"One who has pursued this Mahāyāna for incalculable kalpas, donning the armor of the virtue of precepts and not conceiving of the number of kalpas throughout those countless eons, shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms of the Mahāyāna."
The Bodhisattva Śirigarbha said:
"One who establishes themselves alone and seeks only their own peace cannot attain the universal wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

By relinquishing one's own peace to establish sentient beings, desiring that they find great peace according to their needs, causing them to be without vain expectations or mental arousal, and encouraging the masses to stand firm in the Way and its Dharma—one thus accords with the universal wisdom of the Mahāyāna."
The Bodhisattva Padmaśiri said:
"Noble son! Recall what the Tathāgata has taught:”

"If there were someone who themselves was not gentle and compliant, lacking tranquility and failing to follow the teachings of the discipline, yet wished to tame and tranquilize others or to exhort them with the discipline—such a thing has never occurred."

"Only when one has personally achieved self-discipline, tranquility, and observance of the precepts can one transform and exhort those who are stubborn and unruly, subdue them, and restrain their transgressions; thus shall one accord with the various universal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!"
The Bodhisattva Padma-kośa said:
"Those who are identical with the afflictions of worldly dharmas do not transcend the world;
those who are not identical with the afflictions of worldly dharmas are able to transcend the world."

Therefore, when a bodhisattva remains unmoved and unshaken by gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or insignificance, suffering or pleasure, they shall correspond to the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Dharinīdhara said:

"One cannot attain the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the Great Vehicle from another; I shall proceed alone without a companion. For the sake of sentient beings, I vow to don the armor of virtue; if I protect all, then those whom I ought to lead, deliver, and gather, I shall do so with momentary diligence and without indolence, teaching and transforming the masses to establish them in training—this is what corresponds to the various supernormal knowledges of the Great Vehicle!"
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder said:
"For example, O worthy ones!

All manner of fruits, the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and trees grow because they rely upon the earth. Yet the earth places nothing upon them nor seeks any recompense; all classes of living beings depend upon the earth for their livelihood, yet the earth never tires of them nor considers itself weary."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should also be thus: he should give rise to a mind like the earth, with no attachments; he should not exhort the common people out of likes or dislikes, but lead them toward the Buddha-wisdom without seeking any recompense; only then will he correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Great Vehicle!
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
"Virtuous one, you should know that those who have donned the armor of supreme virtue, up to the wisdom of a Buddha, cannot be thwarted or defeated so as to cause them to abandon the Mahāyāna."

If, even in dreams, one does not set one's mind upon the two vehicles—the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha—but constantly uses the jewel-like mind and the mind of all-encompassing wisdom to preach and proclaim for others; if, regarding this precious jewel-like mind, one has no greed or stinginess and no attachment or parsimony; if one exhorts the multitude toward the Mahāyāna and vows to don the armor of virtue; and if the vehicle thus studied is not a non-existent vehicle, being neither increasing nor decreasing—if one’s mind is such that it harbors no longing or envy, then one shall correspond to the all-encompassing wisdom of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said:
"Beholding the multitudes of sentient beings fallen into the six realms of existence, he gives rise to compassion and bestows upon them the hand of the Dharma;
for those who lack faith, he creates for them the hand of faith."
For those of little wisdom, he is the hand of extensive learning;
for those who are stingy and greedy, he is the hand of generous giving;
for those who violate the precepts, he is the hand that protects the prohibitions.
For those who are angry, he is the hand of patience;
for those who are indolent, he is the hand of diligence;
for those with distracted minds, he is the hand of single-minded concentration.

For those with deviant wisdom, he acts as the hand of true wisdom; yet, following sentient beings who have abandoned the pure and white dharmas, he provides the hand of the Dharma for each according to the time.
The Bodhisattva plants this hand of the roots of merit and seals it within the Three Jewels.
What are the three?
To establish all living beings fully in the Buddha’s wisdom; to encourage and assist them until they reach the hand of the Precious Seal (*ratnamudrā-hasta*);
and once their own roots of virtue are perfected, it is the hand of the Precious Seal.
To contemplate all phenomena as being like empty space is the Hand of the Jewel Seal.
To establish oneself in such a manner constitutes the third [practice], which corresponds to the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:

"Virtuous one, you should know that donning the armor of fearlessness constitutes being without dread. This armor of vowed virtue, the armor of no difficulty, the armor of no obstruction, the armor of no cowardice, and the armor of no indolence—this is the wisdom of the Buddha."

Therefore, the practitioner should not be afraid; being without difficulty or hindrance, without timidity or indolence, free from all trepidation so that the hair on their body does not stand on end, remaining untainted from beginning to end, and neither aspiring to nor looking up toward the virtues of Nirvāṇa, dwelling equally in suffering and pleasure without dualistic conduct—then one accords with the various universal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Siṃhakramavijṛmbhitarāja said:
"Virtuous one, you should know that such a matter is not the conduct of those of inferior capacity; it is something established by true beings."
Those true persons take refuge in equality and remain free from false views;
those true persons possess a sincere and simple mind, devoid of flattery or deceit;
those true persons are diligent, humble, gentle, and compliant, honoring their teachers and revering the sages.
Those who are true practitioners encourage learning without weariness and thoroughly investigate the faculties they have received;
those who are true practitioners revere and delight in right governance and establish right action;
those who are true practitioners, if there are any defiled dharmas to be diminished or abandoned, [they do so].
As for these true men: if they harbor anger, they remain free from resentment;
as for these true men: if they possess delusion, they illuminate and dispel the darkness;
as for these true men: they are tranquil and serene, drawing near to the treasury of meditative concentration.
These true persons are fully endowed with the virtue of giving, providing relief and benefit to all who are poor or in distress, and rescuing them at once;
these true persons guard their body, speech, and mind, remaining profound and tranquil;
these true persons ensure that their words accord with their deeds, and their nature and character are upright and straightforward.
Those true persons are firm and resolute in their aspirations, honoring the Dharma of ultimate truth;
those true persons distance themselves from what is not the Dharma and remain close to the authentic scriptures;
those true persons delight in the joy of the Dharma and protect it through the True Dharma.
These true beings disregard their own bodies and lives without abandoning sentient beings;
these true beings stand firm and resolute, skillfully bestowing gifts without envy;
these true beings are pure and virtuous in their resolve, dissolving all that is wicked and false.
These true beings rescue the poor and destitute with a treasury of jewels;
these true beings act as excellent medicine to cure all ailments;
these true beings protect those who are fearful, enabling them to find refuge.
These true persons lead those with false views to the boundless limit;
these true persons strive to rescue others from toil and defilement, exhorting them with the scriptures;
these true persons harmonize and endure anger, acting in accordance with what is appropriate.
"Therefore, the dharma established for true beings corresponds to the various universal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said:

"One cultivates the immeasurable compassion of empty space; one's diligent practice is never abandoned; through the conduct of great pity, all faculties are joyful and filled with exultation; and regarding all pleasures of desire, one examines them as being like empty space."
If giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are equal to empty space, then one shall accord with the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Thought-Arousing-Turning-the-Wheel-Dharma said:
"Regarding the arousal of the bodhisattva-mind,

that which is aroused should not be such a mind that allows Māra to find an opportunity, nor one that causes the Tathāgata to lack joy, nor one that fails to delight gods and humans, nor one that causes the roots of virtue to diminish."
If one wishes to establish the intention for the Way:

by following and exhorting others accordingly, one shall ensure that the evil Māra finds no opportunity; one will accord with the intent of the Tathāgata so that devas and humans rejoice, and one will not lose the roots of virtue cultivated by oneself.
When one practices in this manner, every arousal of the thought of enlightenment turns the wheel of Dharma. Why is this?
For that bodhisattva, all arisings of thought are produced through causes and conditions yet are without intrinsic birth; they clearly understand that all phenomena are eternally without origination.

That which does not arise is the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas in accordance with true awakening; one who thus resolves their mind and dons the armor of the virtue of the precepts shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva Vibhajyapada said:

"Noble son, you should know that this mind of the Way universally enters into the afflictions of worldly toil, anger, and harm; it enters into the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing, the conditioned and the unconditioned; it also enters into transgression and non-transgression, calamity and merit;
it enters into the wholesome and it enters into the unwholesome."
They also enter into both worldly dharmas and the dharmas that transcend the world;
they also enter into the unconditioned action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) at the beginning and end of existence;
and they also enter into the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
It also enters into the matters of the aggregates (skandhas) and the sense-bases (āyatanas);
it also enters into earth, water, fire, and wind. Why is this so?

All these causes and conditions are spontaneously so; their fundamental nature is inherently pure. In whatever place they may be and whatever they may speak, all that is taught is entirely empty and non-existent.
Just as space penetrates everywhere without exception, so too is the mind of the Way (bodhicitta); it reaches all things universally, bringing joy to all bodhisattvas.

Such a person of wisdom abandons all verbal eloquence and, by discerning the various classes of beings, attains the wisdom of eloquence. If one can enter this single path of noble penetration, then they shall correspond to the various universal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said:

"All that is spoken is ultimately without words, and all sounds are ungraspable. A bodhisattva who delights in such wisdom is neither pleased by pleasant speech nor distressed by unpleasant speech; they are like Mount Sumeru when the wind blows upon it—the wind immediately turns back, yet the mountain remains unmoved."
In this way, the bodhisattva remains unmoved and unshaken by the various heterodox teachings and all their discourses; even amidst various external paths, they remain without attachment.
Whether examining the words of the Tathāgata or the divergent speech of external paths, they do not treat these dharmas with increase or decrease, nor do they become confused by them.
Seeing that all dharmas are exhausted through all forms of eloquence, one does not dwell upon those exhausted dharmas, nor does one conceive of oneself as a deity, nor harbor any thoughts.
A bodhisattva who can practice such wisdom accords with the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:

"A bodhisattva’s entry [into the Dharma] should be like entering the ocean: awakening to the Great Way such that it cannot be reached by any śrāvaka; with faith and joy, focusing the mind single-mindedly on the flavor of the One Dharma; entering into manifold dharmas without perceiving them as manifold;
and contemplating the profound and wondrous Dharma without ever becoming confused."
Regarding the law of dependent origination, there is neither increase nor decrease;
regarding all the sutras, there is no multiplicity—this is what is called "non-arising and non-origination.

As for the activities initiated by all sentient beings, they do not plant the roots of virtue, yet their merit is inexhaustible and their instruction is boundless. One should analytically understand and discard the matters of permanence, neither grasping at phenomena nor severing phenomena. One should establish the will as an immeasurable vessel, never forgetting or abandoning the Dharma, practicing the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) without ever relinquishing the Dharma. Preaching the Dharma of equality for the sake of sentient beings, one should practice all virtuous qualities and wholesome dharmas.

"Thus, being fully endowed with the countless Buddha-dharmas and having donned the armor of the virtue of the precepts with such a mind, one shall correspond to the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Great Mountain said:

"Virtuous One, you should know that this vehicle universally transcends all worlds; it is called the Buddha-wisdom. Its practice and its sphere of entry are immeasurable, and for this reason, it transcends and delivers the mental dispositions of all worlds."
Having already been able to transcend the practices of the world, that which he believes surpasses the mundane;

having already transcended the mundane, his practice of giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom is likewise so, such that he is able to transcend all the wisdom possessed by the world. The merit he creates surpasses the blessings and fortunes produced by the world, and thus he shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"If a bodhisattva encounters forms with his eyes and feels no aversion, the nature of those forms is such that his mind remains pure;
if he hears sounds with his ears and feels no aversion, the nature of those sounds is such that his mind remains pure."

Regarding the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—within these six spheres of sense, there is nothing to be loathed; for these six spheres of sense are by their very nature fundamentally quiescent.
His mind is pure, and he is unattached to feelings of aversion or affection;

his mind is pure, and when observing sentient beings who follow the Buddha-dharma, there is no vessel that he does not respond to. Furthermore, even those sentient beings dwelling in false views, he perceives as vessels for the Buddha-dharma;
and those who love themselves, whether they be kings or those who delight in worldly customs, [he likewise regards].
If one gives a gift and immediately regrets it, their reverence is like this.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they will correspond to the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva King of Joy said:

"Suppose there were someone who reviled, slandered, slighted, insulted, beat, or struck a bodhisattva; yet the bodhisattva harbors no resentment but instead feels joy, treating the opponent with the thought that they are a virtuous friend, and being able to endure with the manifestation of the power of patience, his mind is delighted as he contemplates this Dharma:
'What is it that is being reviled? Who is the one doing the reviling? "

"Having faith and understanding in internal emptiness without doubting external emptiness, one sees one's own body and observes others with joy and delight; thus, one is able to generously bestow one's life, limbs, head, eyes, hands, feet, wife, children, cities, towns, villages, wealth, grain, and precious jewels, leaping for joy all the more."

One would rather hear a single verse and thus cast aside worldly glory and the throne of a universal monarch; one would always delight in preaching the Dharma for others rather than envying Śakra; one would strive to awaken a single person to the Bodhi-mind rather than seeking the status of Brahmā; one would wish to behold the Tathāgata rather than coveting a great trichiliocosm overflowing with precious gems; from birth, one would possess clear understanding and unimpaired faculties, and would faithfully delight in and revere all the factors of the Path.
"One who practices with such joyful delight shall attain the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said:

"If one perceives all dharmas as having crossed to the other shore, does not fall into attachment to the body, purifies all Buddha-lands, beholds all Buddha-fields as equally pure and free from conceptual activity, perceives all Buddhas without giving rise to thoughts of form, and regards all sentient beings [with such equanimity]:"
"Though possessing the fleshly eye, one perceives both transgression and merit with purity;
being fully endowed with the divine eye, one attains indestructibility;
though having attained the wisdom-eye, one remains free from all worldly defilements."
With faith and joy, they fully accomplish the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas;
having attained the Dharma-eye, they are endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
"If a bodhisattva dons the armor of virtue and practices with such faith, they shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Wandering in Boundless Dharma Practice said, "Noble son!
Knowing all that is enacted by the Bodhisattva through conditions, one then fully converges upon all the swift and penetrating wisdoms. Why is this?
Because when one contemplates all existing causes and conditions, they do not abide within, they do not reside without, and they do not exist in verbal expression.
If a bodhisattva does not abide in causes and conditions, nor does he pursue the obstructions of worldly defilement;

if he does not encourage the obstructions of sin and merit, and is free from the obstruction of retribution, the obstruction of the sense faculties, the obstruction of all phenomena, and the obstruction of non-wisdom; having already transcended the realms of sin, merit, dust, and the Māras, then he shall correspond to the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Transcending Mara-Vision said:
"O son of noble family!
If one dwells in the self and perceives a self within one's own body, then one is situated in the activities of Māra."
Having severed the notion of self, one does not perceive what is empty;
having eliminated all views, there are no aggregates (*skandhas*);
having eliminated the aggregates, one does not see Māra.
Having already transcended the realm of Māra, one then attains the gate of unimpeded liberation.
Once a bodhisattva has attained the gate of unimpeded liberation, they shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna!
The Bodhisattva Aśoka-datta said:
"Virtuous one, you should know that those who commit evil will later harbor the torment of boiling water and fire;
those who perform wholesome deeds will later have no sorrow or distress."
Therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate wholesome deeds such that no one can speak ill of what they have done;
whatever they undertake, they shall have no regret later, nor any hindrances or obscurations.
If sentient beings are sorrowful and lack joy, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva then preaches for them the Dharma of transcending sorrow.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices in this manner shall correspond to the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The various counselors said to the Bodhisattva:
"O son of noble family!

Any man who upholds the precepts will surely obtain his aspirations. Having obtained his aspirations, that which he has attained is established through non-negligence; having established non-negligence, he is endowed with the factors of enlightenment."

Having already been able to fully establish the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), one possesses the correctness of the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the precepts of wisdom.
Once a bodhisattva dwells in the dharma of the path free from negligence, they shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Mahāyāna!
The Devaputra Samantakusuma said:
"O son of good family!

When the flowers of a tree are in full bloom, they bring great benefit to all people. A Bodhisattva adorns himself with the roots of merit, just as a tree’s lush blossoms benefit the masses. It is like the Pārijātaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is so profusely and magnificently flowering that none among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa fail to look up to it with reverence."

In this way, the Bodhisattva adorns himself with various Dharma-gates; thus, none among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, or asuras fail to revere him. He is like the bright moon-jewel in the heavens, free from all blemish and fully endowed with manifold virtues.
"If a bodhisattva’s resolve and nature are pure and flawless, and their virtuous reputation is fully manifest, they shall correspond to the various universal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
The Devaputra Prabhāsa said:
"For example, son of good family!..."

When the sun rises, its radiance extinguishes all darkness, manifesting light from beginning to end; so too does the Bodhisattva, fully endowed with the light of wisdom, bestow the gift of the Dharma of wisdom upon the world. For the sake of sentient beings who are ignorant, obscured by darkness, and mired in nescience, he reveals the great light and guides them through the natural Dharma.

That which is shrouded in deep gloom cannot obscure his brilliance; that which is already illuminated by his light is further enabled to dispel darkness. He guides and shows the path, and once they have entered that path, they abide therein.

"If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is on a deviant path, he manifests the correct path; once he has established himself upon the correct path, he shall correspond to the various supernormal knowledges of the Great Vehicle!
The Devaputra Cittakusumagandha said:
"For example, son of good family!..."
The tree of the mind-flower emits a fragrance that universally perfumes an area of forty li; this fragrance is without conceptual thought.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva uses the fragrance of precepts, extensive learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation to create a pervasive incense. Throughout the trichiliocosm, there is no place not reached by the fragrance of the Dharma, and all ailments are healed by this fragrance.
"If a bodhisattva is perfumed by this fragrance of the Dharma, they shall accordingly attain the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the Mahāyāna!
The Devaputra Constantly Advancing in Dharma Practice said:

"Virtuous one, you should know that those who are diligent possess no mind of indolence; therefore, a bodhisattva cultivates the roots of all virtues without weariness, and should always honor and uphold the eightfold practice of the Dharma."

What are the eight? They are: the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni) and pure conduct; traversing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā); gathering and protecting all sentient beings through the four means of integration (catvāri saṃgrahavastūni); aspiring toward the three gates of liberation (trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni) and attaining the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti); exhorting others toward the wisdom of a Buddha; transforming sentient beings to cause them to resolve upon the path to enlightenment; and guiding them through skillful means (upāyakauśalya) to bring them into alignment with all conditioned phenomena. These are the eight.
"By honoring and practicing the eight dharmas, one shall correspond to the various universal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
Thereupon, Mṛdusvara addressed the bodhisattvas and the devaputras, saying:
"O virtuous ones!
If one wishes to know whether a bodhisattva’s diligence is diligent or not diligent regarding the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom— why is this so?
For those who merely habituate themselves to it remain within the three realms, whereas those who follow and cultivate it are said to have attained the vision of the past.
That which is practiced and cultivated is called "internal," while that which is not practiced or cultivated is called "external.
That which is practiced and cultivated refers to the stage of the Śrāvaka; if one follows and cultivates it, it refers to the stage of the Pratyekabuddha.

That which is practiced and cultivated refers to the diligent exertion within the realm of the various fetters; if one follows and cultivates it, it refers to the dharmas of ordinary worldlings to which they are attached.
Those who habitually indulge in it call it "name"; those who practice it in accordance with the Way call it "form.
Those who habitually indulge in it call it "retribution"; those who practice it in accordance with the Way call it "that which is seen.
Those who habitually indulge in it say there is "attachment"; those who practice it in accordance with the Way say there is "attainment."
Those who habitually indulge in them call it "mine," while those who practice them in accordance with the Way call it "my body";
those who habitually indulge in them call it "miserliness and greed," while those who practice them in accordance with the Way call it "generosity without conceit";
those who habitually indulge in them call it "violation of the precepts," while those who practice them in accordance with the Way call it "upholding the precepts without conceit."
Those who habitually indulge in it are said to harbor anger, whereas those who practice it according to the teaching are said to practice patience without conceit;
those who habitually indulge in it are said to be indolent, whereas those who practice it according to the teaching are said to practice diligence without conceit;
those who habitually indulge in it are said to have distracted minds, whereas those who practice it according to the teaching are said to practice single-mindedness without conceit.
Those who indulge in them are said to be deluded; those who follow and cultivate them are said to possess wisdom and do not harbor conceit.
Those who indulge in them are said to lack the roots of goodness; those who follow and cultivate them are said to plant the roots of virtue and do not harbor conceit.
Those who indulge in them are said to lack the roots of merit; those who follow and cultivate them are said to plant the roots of merit and do not harbor conceit.
Those who habitually practice it are said to follow worldly dharmas, while those who respectfully cultivate it are said to follow world-transcending dharmas, yet they harbor no conceit;
those who habitually practice it are said to follow conditioned dharmas, while those who respectfully cultivate it are said to follow unconditioned dharmas, yet they harbor no conceit;
those who habitually practice it are said to commit offenses, while those who respectfully cultivate it are said to follow offense-free dharmas, yet they harbor no conceit.
Those who habitually practice it are said to possess outflows (*āsrava*); those who cultivate it according to the precepts are said to be without outflows and free from conceit.

This is called progressing from habitual practice to cultivation, thereby departing from all views. When one neither clings to nor abandons the bodhisattva’s guiding principle, one then accords with the various supernormal wisdoms of the Mahāyāna!
"Furthermore, O worthy one!
One cannot yet attain the various forms of universal wisdom.
For what reason does one not attain them?"
By what means does one attain the various supernormal knowledges and wisdom?

Those who possess these supernormal knowledges and wisdoms are free from all conditioned activities; those supernormal knowledges and wisdoms themselves have no destination, nor is there anyone who attains them.
Furthermore, all supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) are likewise without form or appearance, and they are without the characteristics of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
these supernormal knowledges are neither subject to dharma nor subject to non-dharma.
Furthermore, those various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms are themselves without giving.
Why is this? Because those who possess the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms are themselves the act of giving.
Furthermore, in all supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) there is no morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, or wisdom.
Why is this? Because those who possess supernormal knowledges are naturally noble ones (ārya).
Those who possess the various supernormal knowledges have no past, future, or present. Why is this?
Because those various supernormal knowledges transcend the three periods of time.
Those who possess all-encompassing wisdom have no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mental consciousness. Why is this?
Because they have transcended all realms.
"O virtuous ones!

If you wish to know the various supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), and if there is a bodhisattva who desires to attain these supernormal knowledges and abide in accordance with them, how should they abide?
They should abide in non-abiding toward all phenomena; this is what constitutes abiding."
Regarding all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and all dharmas, none are "mine"; these supernormal knowledges have no attachment or clinging toward any dharma.
These supernormal knowledges are equal to the stage of ordinary beings and equal to the stage of a Buddha; they are likewise equal regarding all dharmas.
Furthermore, one who practices these supernormal knowledges as a bodhisattva should not seek them elsewhere.
All supernormal wisdoms should be sought from these four great elements as the spontaneous formation of practice. Why is this?
That which is "spontaneous" is this very non-existence.
That which is spontaneous has no form; therein, the wholesome dharmas are called "my body.
Regarding this "my body," there is no body, no good or evil, no self, no life-span, no vital principle, and no person.

If my own body were non-existent and likewise absent, then there would be no activity and nothing at all; whatever form it may have would likewise lack reality. That which is perceived would also be non-existent and devoid of reality. When wisdom perceives that what exists is non-existent, and that both existence and non-existence are equal—such wisdom is the wisdom of universal penetration!

When the youth Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and twelve thousand people all resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Chapter Two: On the Emanated Buddhas (Part One). At that time, the Bodhisattva Vidyutkūṭa addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Let us go together to visit the Tathāgata and inquire face-to-face with the Great Sage:
'What practices should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva undertake?'"
Mañjuśrī immediately manifested a Tathāgata at that spot, his physical form and appearance identical to those of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta then addressed Prajñākūṭa, saying:
"Noble son!..."
"The Tathāgata is here; why do you not inquire about the practices established by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas?
Thereupon, Prajñākūṭa questioned the manifested Tathāgata: "Indeed."
“World-Honored One!
What practices should a bodhisattva mahāsattva undertake?
At that time, the Buddha told him:
"As I have established, so too should a bodhisattva practice such conduct.
He asked again:
"What is the conduct established by the World-Honored One?"
That Buddha replied:
"One does not practice giving, nor practice moral discipline, nor practice patience, nor practice diligence, nor practice single-minded concentration, nor practice wisdom."
They do not course in the desire realm, they do not course in the form realm, and they do not course in the formless realm.
They do not perform bodily formations, they do not perform verbal formations, and their minds have no mental formations.
That all things are without activity and without causes or conditions is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Noble son, what do you think?
Does that which is a magical manifestation possess any activity?
He replied:
"O God among Gods!
That which is a transformation has no activity."
He replied, “It is so,
son of good family!”
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should perform such deeds.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Is the Buddha you have seen not perhaps a transformation?”
Mañjuśrī replied, "Virtuous one!
Have you not heard that all dharmas are transformations of the natural state?"
"It is like the appearance of a magical illusion, yet one does not regress. He replied, "It is so!"
"All dharmas are truly transformations; they naturally undergo illusory changes without ever regressing.
He replied:
"Now, son of good family!"
Why do you say:
"Is it not that the Tathāgata now appearing has undergone transformation?
Are not all Buddhas and all dharmas likewise subject to transformation?"
He asked again:
"Who is the one who creates these transformations? He replied:
"It is simply through the purification of natural karma that one transforms others.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva should not dwell upon the notions of self, person, life, or soul, nor upon the noble path of a Buddha or that of an ordinary person, nor should they calculate that there is any such dwelling."
Vetragupta asked the manifested Tathāgata:
"World-Honored One!
What must one study to personally attain Buddhahood?"
He replied:
"That which has nothing to be learned is the training of a bodhisattva.
What the bodhisattva trains in has no form or image, nor does it have any peer."
Neither receiving anything nor not receiving;
neither having conceptualization nor being free from conceptualization;
neither having any practice nor practicing or not practicing—this is the training of a bodhisattva.
Without attachment and without non-attachment; without pride and without non-pride;
nor engaging in frivolous play; neither practicing nor abandoning practice;
without conceptualization and without grasping; without a place of dwelling, and without even the notion of such a place.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going;
without abiding and without transformation, without form and without words—universally free from all conceptualizations and mental activities, such is the training of a bodhisattva.
To practice this study is to engage in the study of equality.
One who practices this study has no destination, neither increases nor decreases;

one who practices this study is neither attached, nor liberated, nor defiled, nor detached from dust, nor harbors resentment. Such a person does not fall into ignorance; to study in this manner is truly called "study."
One who studies in this manner does not go to the various realms of existence.
Therefore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain and perfect the unsurpassed, right, and true path should study what I have studied.
He asked again:
"What is the study of the Buddha? He replied:
"Just as I have no precepts, so too I have no transgressions.
There is no giving and no receiving; no precepts and no transgressions; no patience and no anger; no diligence and no laziness; no meditation and no distraction; no wisdom and no folly."
Neither a learner nor a non-learner, there is nothing that is not practiced, yet I have no attainment and nothing with which to be equaled;
there is no Buddha and no Dharma;
furthermore, there is no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a life-sustaining being, no notion of a life-principle, and no notion of a phenomenon.
There is neither perception nor non-perception.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely unconditioned.
All dharmas are unconditioned, naturally like illusions, without characteristics and without duality;
all dharmas are free from all that is cherished;
all dharmas are invisible.
All dharmas transcend the gateway of the eye.
All dharmas are equal and without distinction;
all dharmas are ignorant and dark, having no path, being unconditioned and devoid of a person. Therefore, there is no teaching of a person, and therefore there is no location.
Where there is no verbal teaching, there is nothing that arises.
One who believes this does not dwell upon what they believe, nor do they become conceited, nor do they dwell upon the Way.
Therefore, son of good family!
"If there is a bodhisattva who trains in the Buddha-way in such a manner, being neither terrified nor fearful, neither daunted nor afraid, they are indeed a bodhisattva!
O son of good family!"

The fearlessness of space: it fears not fire, it fears not wind, it fears not rain, it fears not mist, it fears not dust, it fears not thunder, it fears not clouds, it fears not lightning, and it fears not snow.
Why is this? Because emptiness is spontaneous, it is called "fearlessness regarding emptiness.
In this way, the bodhisattva is without fear toward any phenomenon and does not dwell upon suffering or pleasure regarding any phenomenon.

If a bodhisattva’s mind is thus equanimous, they will be able to attain Buddhahood and subdue all Māras; they will realize the unsurpassed, true, and correct path as the Most Perfectly Awakened One, and will also be able to guide and benefit all sentient beings.
When the emanated Tathāgata had finished speaking these words, he immediately vanished, and his whereabouts were unknown.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa asked Mañjuśrī:
"Where has the Tathāgata gone now?"
He replied, "From where I came.
He asked again:
“From where have you come? He replied,
“From the same place as your destination.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
That which is manifested through transformation comes from nowhere and goes nowhere?"
He replied: "Noble son!
For example, just as a magical creation comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, so too it is with all dharmas!"
"All sentient beings are equal and without distinction; they neither come nor go.
He asked again, "Mañjuśrī!"
"To what do all dharmas tend?
He replied,
"They tend toward spontaneity."
He asked again:
"To what do all sentient beings return? He replied:
"Act according to what you have done.
He asked again, "Mṛdvin!"
"All dharmas are without action and without retribution?
He replied, "Noble son!"
"That which is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is without action, without retribution, and without going; to impartially govern all phenomena is what constitutes the Dharma-realm.
He asked again:
"How can one say that there is action, retribution, and going, yet claim there is no going?"
He replied:
"Noble son! Just as they act and just as they receive retribution, so too is their destination."
He asked Mṛdvinśa again,
"What is meant by 'action,' and what is its retribution?"
"For what reason do you go?
He replied, "As that which is performed is such, so too is its retribution; as that which is performed is such, so too is that to which one goes."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
That which is like the absence of a fundamental basis—does it also have no action, no retribution, and no destination?"
He replied:
"O son of noble family!
Just as that which has no origin has nothing created, nothing resulting in retribution, and nothing toward which one proceeds."
The same applies to actions, their retributions, and the destinies to which one goes: there is neither coming nor going;
these actions, retributions, and the places reached are like that which has no origin and no destination.

When these words were spoken, as if in the presence of the World-Honored One, the Buddha Śākyamuni, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Ānanda, and the other great disciples all heard this discourse.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“So be it, Tathāgata!”
How extraordinary and unprecedented!

These true sons of the noble ones are great sages who, while uttering the lion’s roar within the same single Dharma, employ various kinds of sounds and speech that accord perfectly with the assembly of the Dharma without any error.
"Who, upon hearing this, would not resolve to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is truly as you have said.

Because the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva is free from hindrance, what is now spoken is likewise free from hindrance. Just as one sows, so shall one surely reap the fruit; and just as one produces [the cause], so too shall the retribution be."

When a bodhisattva trains in this way without hindrance, they explain with discernment through their noble wisdom; just as Śāriputra’s own training was in the prohibitions, so too is his wisdom and eloquence.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī asked the World-Honored One:
“What is called the training of the śrāvaka?
What is called the training of the bodhisattva?”
The Buddha said:
"That which is limited and obstructed is the training of the śrāvaka; that which is limitless and unobstructed is the training of the bodhisattva.
Because the training of the śrāvaka is constrained by limitations, it results in obstruction; for this reason, what is taught is limited and leads to obstruction."
"Furthermore, because the training of all bodhisattvas is limitless and leads to non-obstruction, that which they proclaim is likewise limitless and without obstruction.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī then addressed the Buddha,
saying, "O World-Honored One, O God among Gods!"

I pray that you will manifest a responsive miracle so that these worthy gentlemen may come here, and that those in this assembly may hear the Dharma being taught, each attaining their own goal so that their presence here is not in vain.
"Why is this? Because the conduct of the youth Mañjuśrī is profound, and the sūtras and dharmas he discusses are likewise essential and subtle.
At that moment, the World-Honored One manifested a portentous response.
At that moment, Mṛdumati, together with twenty-five virtuous men and various devaputras, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāśuddhi addressed Mṛdumati, saying:
"O Virtuous One!..."
"Why have you bypassed the assembly of the Tathāgata to discourse on the sutras in private?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Noble son!..."

Knowing that the Tathāgata is most venerable and beyond challenge, and because all the Buddhas and Great Sages have for this reason declared that whatever is spoken may be feared as unassailable, they remain to one side.
He asked again:
"Mṛdumati! What Dharma can you preach that would be worthy of a Tathāgata?"
Mṛdusvara replied,
"As I have spoken, so shall the World-Honored One know it.
Prabhāśrī said:
"Even so, I pray that you will explain its meaning. He replied:
"According to what I have attained, I shall now proclaim and manifest it."
"O son of noble family!

If what you have said does not contravene the realm of reality (dharmadhātu), does not lose its original non-being, and does not lose the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), then such speech may indeed be considered that of a Tathāgata!"

Furthermore, if what is spoken has no principle for dispute, no ground for reproach, and nothing to be undertaken; if it is without causes and conditions, without form or appearance, and without analogy—then one who speaks in such a manner accords with and follows the Tathāgata!

There is no likeness of a self, nor the form of another; there is no appearance of equal dharmas, no appearance of non-dharmas, no appearance of beginning or end, and no appearance of nirvana. One who speaks thus may be called a Tathāgata!
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Mṛdvinśa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have spoken these words most skillfully."
It is exactly as you have said; one who speaks thus does not contradict the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose one is entirely free from all worldly play and delight, remaining undisturbed; if one does not insistently dwell upon various perceptions, being without manifold conceptions; if that which is spoken proceeds with tranquility and without fluctuation; if one dons the armor of a single virtue and preaches the Dharma with a concentrated mind, such that no one can destroy or corrupt their scripture; and if one perceives no phenomenon whatsoever as increasing or decreasing—one who speaks in this manner may indeed be called a Tathāgata.
When these words were spoken, eight hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Chapter Three:

Raising the Alms Bowl (Part One) At that time, there were twelve hundred devaputras in the assembly who had previously practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva; however, they had forgotten their resolve for the Way and their will was not firm.

They thought to themselves: "The Buddha’s wisdom is sublime and immeasurable; the mind set upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path is difficult to attain; that which is studied by bodhisattvas is beyond reach; and the state of supreme perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to obtain."

"We are unable to accomplish this practice; it would be better for us to seek instead the path of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha and attain extinction. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of these sons of heaven—that they were capable of accomplishing the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become Most Perfectly Enlightened Ones, yet wished to abandon it midway to take up the Lesser Vehicle—[spoke thus].

Desiring to exhort and transform the various devaputras, the Buddha departed from the site of enlightenment and, manifesting as an elder before the assembly, held a bowl filled with a hundred kinds of food and drink in his hands and brought it to the Buddha’s presence. He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the Great Sage will take pity on me and accept this meal."
The Buddha then took the bowl.
Mṛdusvara Bodhisattva approached the Buddha’s presence, joined his palms in reverence, and said:
“Now that you partake of this sumptuous meal, you should remember your former kindness.”

I have heard with sincere faith that although the Great Sage partakes of food, he does not extend the benefit of the Dharma to those as lowly as us; it would be most fitting for him to bestow such grace upon us, thereby restoring his former intention to favor us with the Dharma.
Thereupon, the venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"What past kindness or virtue does Mṛdvinīśa possess that, in the presence of the World-Honored One, he speaks of looking back upon the grace of the Dharma even while eating?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What past kindness did the youth Mañjuśrī have toward the Great Sage, that he would place the Tathāgata [in this position], saying:
'Even when one is about to eat, one should reflect upon the kindness of former dharmas'?"
The Buddha told him:
"Wait a moment; he shall depart of his own accord. What the Tathāgata knows is not within your reach.
Thereupon, the Buddha immediately set the bowl down upon the ground, and the bowl sank downward, traveling through various buddha-fields.

The Buddhas who are currently existing as Perfectly Awakened Ones each see their almsbowls descend beneath their feet; they travel downward through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers until they reach the realm of the Tathāgata King of Radiance, whose world is named Illumination.
The bowl remained in that place in mid-air, standing there naturally without anyone to hold it.
To whichever Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples it went, each approached and questioned their World-Honored One:
"From where has this bowl come?"
Each of the Buddhas spoke to explain their intention, saying:
"In the world-system above, named Endurance (Sahā), there is a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni who currently teaches the Dharma."
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni has intentionally descended with this bowl, wishing to exhort and transform those bodhisattvas whose resolve has faltered.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Go and seek the bowl; once you have ascertained its location, go and bring it here."

Immediately accepting the instruction, he relied upon his own power of wisdom to carry out the Buddha’s holy intent; entering into samādhi with perfect concentration, he transcended ten thousand buddha-lands in a single moment of meditative absorption, searching everywhere for the bowl, yet could not find its whereabouts.
He returned and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
I sought it but could not see it; I do not know where it is."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“Go now and seek out the bowl; examine its location to see in which direction it lies.

Having received these instructions, Maudgalyāyana employed his supernormal powers to carry out the Buddha’s holy intent; entering into samādhi and attaining eight thousand concentrations, he suddenly traversed eight thousand buddha-fields. Yet, though he searched, he did not see it and knew not its whereabouts. He returned and reported to the Buddha:
"If I exhaust my supernatural powers and yet do not receive the bowl, how could I possibly bring it here?
The World-Honored One again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Go and seek the bowl; once you know where it has gone, search for it and bring it back."

He immediately followed these instructions and entered into samādhi, attaining twelve thousand concentrations. In a trance-like state, he transcended twelve thousand Buddha-lands, yet he searched for the bowl without finding it and knew not where it had come to rest.

In this manner, these five hundred great śrāvakas, remaining in the air, each manifested the power of their supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*) and meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), as well as the divine majesty of their spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) and the far-reaching vision of their divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Each went forth to seek their alms-bowls, yet they did not know where they were, nor could they find them.
Then Subhūti stepped forward and addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

"Virtuous One, you are of lofty talent and in your final birth before Buddhahood; as the Tathāgata has prophesied, you shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become a most perfectly awakened Buddha!"

His benevolence and grace are vast, and his wisdom is so profound and far-reaching that it surpasses all others; he walks alone through the three realms without peer. You should know that as for the bowl, only he can retrieve it and bring it here for you to offer!
"I am fortunate that you have condescended to honor me by accepting this bowl.
Maitreya Bodhisattva replied to Subhūti:
"It is truly as you say; having received the wisdom of the Tathāgata, one shall surely attain perfect enlightenment!"
Now, as for the concentration of mind that Mṛdvinaya has aroused—his advancing, halting, sitting, and rising are beyond my reach;
I am unable to fully comprehend this samādhi. Truly, Subhūti!

Although I shall attain Buddhahood in a future age, with a multitude of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all shall be led by the path opened by Mṛdvinīśa; yet if one wishes to know the thoughts arising at the lifting of a single step, one will not recognize where they lead.
"Therefore, O Benevolent One, you should request Mṛdumati!
Only this Great Being knows the location of the bowl and the land where it resides; he is capable of bringing it here.
Then Subhūti addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I pray that you will bestow your compassionate instruction.
Thereupon, the Great Sage dispatched Maitreya to fetch the bowl.
Receiving this command, Maitreya reflected within himself:

"I shall bring forth this bowl without rising from my seat and without leaving the assembly."—This samādhi of Mṛdusvara is called "Universal Transcendence" (Samantātikrama); it is the meditative absorption and right attainment of all bodhisattvas.

At that time, Mṛdvinaya extended his right palm and plunged it into the earth, passing down through the lower realms; as he proceeded, he bowed his head in succession before each and every one of the Buddhas, the infinite Great Sages, whom he encountered.
From within his palm, a voice spontaneously issued, saying:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni respectfully inquires after you: Are you free from ailment?
Are you well and vigorous? Is your strength as usual? Do you dwell in peace?"

From every single pore of his palms and arms, there spontaneously issued forth hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of radiant lights; each of these lights manifested hundreds of thousands of lotus flowers.
Within each lotus flower, a Tathāgata appeared, fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, sitting cross-legged upon the flower.
Each of these World-Honored Ones individually extolled the name, virtue, and meritorious achievements of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
In all the Buddha-lands he traversed, at that moment the various kingdoms shook in six ways.
Furthermore, a natural great radiance pervaded all the Buddha-lands without exception, and in every one of those Buddha-lands, this palm appeared.

Furthermore, in all those Buddha-fields, silken streamers, banners, pennants, and various canopies were naturally suspended, such that there was nothing that was not magnificently adorned; flowers were scattered everywhere, decorating every place.

After Mṛdusvara had passed through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers with his palm to pay homage to the Buddhas, in an instant he suddenly arrived at the world called Ābhāsvara, the land of the Buddha Prabhāsavat. Having finished his prostrations, a great voice spontaneously issued forth, saying:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni respectfully inquires after the welfare of the Tathāgata Amitaprabhāsavat!"
There was an attendant bodhisattva named Prabhāśrī who addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
“What is this palm?
It is exquisite, sublime, and its majestic spiritual power is beyond compare; it spontaneously emits hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of radiant beams of light.”
From each and every ray of light, there emanated hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of pure and adorned lotus flowers;
upon each lotus flower sat a Tathāgata, extolling the meritorious achievements of the Sage, the Honored One of Benevolence.
The Buddha Prabhāpāla said to Prabhāśrī:
"O son of noble family!

To the north, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in seventy-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world-system called Sahā. There, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni currently dwells and teaches the Dharma."

There was a great being named Maitreya, who had donned the inconceivable armor of the virtue of the precepts and possessed the infinite power of all supernatural penetrations; remaining seated without moving from his place, he extended his palm and came forward, wishing to lift the bowl and return it.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas in the buddha-field of King Prabhāsa all felt a deep yearning and longing, desiring to behold the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī of that Sahā world.

The Buddha King of Radiant Light, fully knowing the thoughts and visions within the assembled multitude, immediately emitted a ray of light from the mark between his eyebrows and the crown of his head. This light shone through seventy-two Ganges-river-sands of Buddha-lands, reaching upward to the Sahā world-system, such that there was nowhere it did not brilliantly illuminate.
Any sentient beings who were graced by this light all attained peace and were free from all afflictions, like the Universal Monarch, the Wheel-Turning Sage King;
those practitioners who were single-mindedly devoted to the study of meditative concentration, upon being touched by this light, all attained the traces of the Path;
and those who had attained dhyāna all transcended the three realms and realized the four fruits of sanctity.
Those whose outflows were exhausted attained the eight gates of liberation;
the Arhats in meditative concentration attained the source of non-attachment;
and those Bodhisattvas whose bodies were illuminated by light all universally attained the Sunlight Samādhi.

In this manner, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Prabhāsavat saw this Sahā world-system, including the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the youth Mañjuśrī, the entire assembly of holy śrāvaka bhikṣus, and all the bodhisattvas.
Upon beholding the assembly of bodhisattvas in the Sahā world, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa immediately shed tears and spoke these words, addressing the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
Just as a wondrous crystal or wish-fulfilling gem would be truly pitiable if it were to fall into impurity,
so too are these bodhisattvas who are born in the Realm of Endurance (Sahā-lokadhātu) most deeply to be commiserated.
The Buddha Prabhāpāla said to Prabhāśrī, "Do not speak such words. Why is this? Because..."

To practice the cultivation of dhyāna with diligence in this buddha-field for ten kalpas is not as good as, in the Sahā world, giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for sentient beings from dawn until the time of the morning meal; the merit of this is supreme, peerless, and difficult to equal.

The Bhikṣu Prajñārāja instructed the young children, saying:

Leisure is difficult to encounter; one should likewise resolve their intent with sincerity.

when wisdom reaches the ultimate limit, who would not give rise to the aspiration for the Way?

The Tathāgata’s attainment of noble awakening, his boundless wisdom, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of unimpeded wisdom—all are the grace of Mañjuśrī’s exhortation.

Some dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven;

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

The Buddha had two foremost disciples among his śrāvakas: one named Chao-shu (Visheshagamin), whose wisdom was towering and sublime;

He is a field of merit for the world, his radiance so brilliant and magnificent as to be beyond compare; we should all together offer him worship, for those who present offerings will receive vast and great blessings and joy.

A field of merit beyond compare;
"When one makes offerings and provides all manner of worship, one bestows this immeasurable blessing.

"What wise person, possessing clear insight, would see this and feel any stinginess?

"Having liberated immeasurable aspirations, they abide in the dharma of equality.

Then the two youths said to one youth:

A youth replied:

Like the stride of a lion,
illuminating the great assembly, my body vows to be thus!
Supreme and foremost in the three realms, I shall deliver all beings throughout the ten directions.
At that time, as soon as this young boy had finished speaking these words, eight thousand devaputras in the sky simultaneously praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
"Speak these words quickly! Now that you have resolved your mind [on enlightenment], both the heavens and the world shall receive your protection.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"At that time, by the side of the Tathāgata Sarvadarśin, there was an attendant named Sāgaramati, who was most eminent for his vast learning. The Buddha then addressed him, saying:"

"The God among Gods!

"Even when you are reborn in the Brahma Heaven as a Brahmā King, it shall be just so!
With each step you take, the root of merit shall cause you to behold a hundred Buddhas.
At that time, the three young boys went to where the Tathāgata Sarvadarśin was, prostrated at his feet, and scattered jeweled necklaces over the World-Honored One.

The pearl necklace scattered by that one youth, who had conceived the mind of universal supernormal wisdom, stayed in the air above the Buddha and transformed into a multi-storied pavilion with latticed windows, tiered galleries, and curtains, standing four-sidedly and surrounded by equal adornments; within it was manifested a bed and seat, upon which the Tathāgata sat.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Sarvārthasiddha immediately smiled with joy.
His attendant asked, “Indeed, World-Honored One! Why do you smile?”
"For what reason do you smile? A smile must have its purpose.
The Tathāgata replied, "Sāgaramati!..."
"Do you see these two youths who have conceived the aspiration for the vehicle of the śrāvakas, scattering pearl necklaces upon the Tathāgata?

"O Great Sage!

The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Do you harbor doubts in your mind?

The boy on the right side was Śāriputra;

Observe that when you were first afraid of the perils of birth and death, although you planted roots of virtue, you were unable to give rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment; your will was timid and weak, and you desired only swift extinction rather than rapid transcendence.
