Your friends have become disciples of the Buddha and thereby attained liberation; for this reason, you should form this contemplation:
if anyone wishes to achieve nirvana, they should resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Why is this so? That which is called "supreme speed" refers to the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) that none can surpass; it is truthful and without deception, its vehicle is foremost, and it brings universal peace to all classes of living beings—this is precisely what the various supernormal knowledges are.
It is the most subtle, exceptionally honored, and unsurpassed;
it is peerless and without equal;
it is without rival and cannot be surpassed. It is the vehicle of non-obstruction, which no vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can reach; this is called the Vehicle of Universal Wisdom.
When the Buddha preached this Mahāyāna Dharma-text, ten thousand people conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that moment, those great śrāvakas—the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Revata, Ānanda, Kātyāyanīputra, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and the Venerable Subhūti—prostrated themselves on the ground, bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and together addressed the World-Honored One:
“Indeed it is so, O Great Sage!”

If sons or daughters of good family have resolved upon the Great Mind, they should provide offerings to them; for this is the subtle and wondrous state of liberation and the practice of the Truly Real. Why is this so?

Even if hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were to preach to us the practices of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), we would lack the capacity and power to undertake them. The mind set upon all-encompassing wisdom is unimpeded for those who possess all wisdom; it is supreme and difficult to equal. We would rather commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and remain in the Avīci Hell without ceasing, than abandon the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*) to become mere śrāvakas.

Why is this so? Even if one commits a heinous crime and falls into hell to undergo various bitter sufferings, once those pains have come to an end, one will emerge from hell without being far removed [from liberation].

With a mind of unimpeded supernormal wisdom, one considers what could possibly be given now, finding nothing fit or harmonious; having burned away the source of the true and right and brought its roots to ruin, such a person lacks the vessel of a Buddha regarding this unhindered wisdom of the Buddha’s insight.
Just as a man who has passed away provides no benefit to his relatives, so it is with us:
by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle we aspire for liberation, abandoning all things and providing no benefit to sentient beings.
Just as this earth provides abundant nourishment for all living beings— whether they have two feet, four feet, or many feet— so it is,
World-Honored One!
Those who resolve to attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path receive grace and achieve liberation throughout the heavens above and the world below.

Chapter 5: On the Absence of Self (Middle Section). At that time, when the World-Honored One had nearly finished expounding this account from beginning to end, King Ajātaśatru mounted a chariot drawn by four horses and led his fourfold army—elephants, chariots, cavalry, and infantry—to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“O Heaven among Heavens! [...]”
In what do sentient beings abide? What serves as their basis and cause?
By what conditions do they arise?
And by what means do they incur transgressions?
The Buddha said to the king:

"Those who dwell in the notions of self, person, life, and soul, by means of these, sentient beings create offenses and transgressions; relying on and clinging to the body of greed, they give rise to inverted conditions, and through this, the multitudes of living beings bring about calamities and afflictions."
He asked again:
"Wherein lies the root cause of that which craves the body?
The World-Honored One replied:
"That which is greed for the body has a lack of wisdom as its root.
He asked again:
"What is that which lacks wisdom rooted in?"
He replied:
"The objects of one's thoughts that are unwholesome factors are their root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of the factors of wrong thought?
He replied: "Deceit is the root."
He asked again:
"What is the root of falsehood?
He replied:
"Those thoughts that lack reality are the root.
He asked again:
"In what way are those thoughts that lack reality the root?"
He replied, "It is said that non-existence and non-perception are the faculty.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the absence of non-existence and non-perception'?
He replied: "To say that there is no arising and no existence—this is called non-perception."
He asked again:
"If it is neither produced nor existent, how should one conceive of it?
In what place does its numerical category reside?"
He replied,
"That which is neither born nor existent has no conceptualization.
He asked again:
"From what causes and conditions does doubt arise?
He replied:
"That which is doubt arises from hesitation."
He asked again:
"What is this state of hesitation?
He replied:
"To hear the truthful words spoken by the noble sages and yet harbor doubt upon hearing them—this is called hesitation.
He asked again:
"What are the noble sages, and what are their words that are considered authentic and true?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"That which is called 'noble' refers to the elimination of all craving and views;
that which is called 'thoroughly discerning' refers to knowing that all phenomena are entirely non-existent."
King Ajātaśatru addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"That which is called 'the noble and holy state of non-possession' is in fact a falsehood. World-Honored One, you abide in that which has already exhausted the dust of afflictions, yet you establish and create attachments within the world. Regarding what the various noble ones have preached, my mind remains in doubt, and I have incurred immeasurable sins and calamities."
"O World-Honored One!
My father was without fault and had committed no transgression, yet his life was endangered.

Because of greed for the kingdom or for wealth and treasures, he became deluded by honor and nobility and neglected his estate; addicted to profit, he oppressed the people and plotted treason. Holding onto these doubts, he was struck with terror and could find no peace, as if amidst a joyful gathering or playful amusement."
Whether he was in the inner palace sporting with his ladies-in-waiting;
or whether he was sitting or lying down, engaged in making judicial decisions;

or whether he was in seclusion listening to and reviewing state affairs or presiding over his ministers—day and night he was filled with anxiety and trepidation, unable to cast off the knots of his lingering reflections.
He has no appetite for food or drink; though there be exquisite delicacies, he finds them not sweet.

His eyes are dim and what he beholds is blurred; his countenance is haggard and his mind is constantly trembling with anxiety, finding no peace in his dwelling, as he fears that after his life ends he will fall into hell.
I look up with reverence to the Tathāgata!
You are able to cause those who are terrified to be free from fear;
you bestow the gift of eyes upon those who are blind and in darkness.
He rescues those who are sinking;
he causes those who encounter suffering and affliction to attain great peace;
and he receives as his refuge those who have no place to turn.
He provides relief to those who have no protector;
he bestows wealth and livelihoods upon those who are impoverished;
and he administers medical treatment to those who are ill.
To those who have fallen onto deviant paths, he shows the correct way;
toward those already on the correct path, he gives rise to great compassion.
His mind endures toil without regarding it as a hardship, equally pitying all the common people with firm and ultimate compassion from beginning to end, remaining unmoved by pleasure or pain.
“The Tathāgata arises to rescue and deliver sentient beings, leaving none behind and not abandoning a single person.
O World-Honored One, our sole refuge!

Grant us your grace and consolation to remove our fear and anxiety. We are orphaned with no savior; act as our savior alone. Let those who are hungry and thirsty obtain full satisfaction; we are now exhausted and on the verge of collapsing to the ground, and pray only that you will support and sustain us.”
Now that I have nowhere to turn, I pray that you will accept me as your follower;
now that I am already sinking, I pray that you will grant me rescue and deliverance, so that my body may not fall into the great hells, down to the Avīci Hell.
"Indeed, Great Sage!
Please preach the Dharma as it truly is to resolve my doubts, to untie the knots of sorrow so that there is no more hesitation, and to cause these heavy offenses to become light."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"King Ajātaśatru’s speech is sagacious and most subtle; the Dharma he has entered is exceedingly profound and vast. No one else is capable of resolving his doubts and leaving no remaining fetters; only Maitreya (Niu-shou) can clear away these obstructions."
Then Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, addressed King Ajātaśatru:

“If you wish to resolve your doubts, you should prepare a sumptuous feast and invite the youthful Mañjuśrī. He shall then sever the knots of your kingliness, your afflictions, and your suspicions, bringing peace and stability to the kingdom and the inner palace. He will accept the king’s couches and various offerings; the ladies of the inner palace, the court attendants, and all followers shall obtain immeasurable merit, and countless sentient beings throughout the great kingdom of Rājagṛha and Magadha shall all attain prosperity through this deliberation.”
King Ajātaśatru then stepped forward and addressed the youthful Mañjuśrī:
"I pray that you will deign to show compassion and accept a modest meal along with your retinue.
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Great King, please stop!
We have already received sufficient offerings.
Within the True Dharma and Vinaya, there is no such record as this: that one should accept robes or food and drink while hoping for further compassion.”
The King then asked again:
"How should one manifest and present this deep red? Ruci replied:
"Suppose, Great King!

Upon hearing this profound, wondrous, and extraordinary discourse on the truth, you feel no fear, no terror, no dread, no trepidation, no anxiety, and no apprehension—then you shall be granted compassion."
Furthermore, Great King!
One does not think upon dharmas, nor is it non-thought; being without thought and without non-thought—to practice in this way is what constitutes compassion.
"Even so, Great King!

Not conceiving a mind that goes, yet not being without such conception; not thinking of a mind that comes, yet not being without such thought; and having no grasping even toward the present mind—this is what constitutes the addition of compassion."
"Furthermore, Great King!
Not falling into false views and yet not extinguishing them;
neither having anything seen nor anything unseen—this is what constitutes the extension of compassion."
King Ajātaśatru again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What has been spoken now is entirely in accordance with the Dharma; I pray that you will take pity on me and accept my invitation."
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Your Majesty, you should know this!
As recorded in the laws and teachings, one does not bestow offerings of alms-food, clothing, or meals as acts of grace."
"Furthermore, Great King, if one does not conceive of a self,
does not conceive of a person, does not conceive of a life-span, and does not conceive of a soul, it is only then that one may be moved by compassion and accept offerings and gifts."
Suppose, Great King!
One does not cherish one's own body nor cherish others, and is entirely without grasping—this is what constitutes the exercise of compassion.
Suppose, Great King!

Not withdrawing the mind, not calculating causes and conditions, and not abiding in the matters of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*); having no internal phenomena and no external phenomena; not accepting the three realms and not transcending the three realms; having neither good nor evil, neither virtue nor non-virtue; not dwelling in the world and yet not transcending the world; having neither sin nor merit; being neither with outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without outflows; being neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); not abandoning birth and death and not accepting extinction (*nirvāṇa*)—this is called "adding compassion" (*anukampā*).
The King replied:
"Indeed, Niu-shou! I shall receive and accept such a discourse on the Dharma;
for this reason, I pray that you would grant me your request, out of compassion and pity for those of inferior capacity."
Niu-shou replied:
"O King, you should understand this!

If all dharmas were to have anything upon which to rely, anything to be received, anything to be attained, or anything to be protected, then one would not receive compassion and could not reach peace."

If one were to have attachment toward phenomena and form conceptualizations, or were to establish a dwelling place and become negligent, all would be protected by that attachment to conceptualizations, that dwelling place, and that negligence.
"Suppose, Great King!

One’s aspirations are ultimately fulfilled and one reaches the ultimate eternal peace, free from all affliction; yet, were you, Great King, to engage in further actions, you would not be sustained by compassion and would fail to attain tranquility."
King Ajātaśatru again asked Mañjuśrī:
"By receiving what Dharma does one become free from affliction and reach the state of non-existence?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"If one thoroughly understands emptiness, there is nothing that is done, nor is there anything that is not done;
there is no perception and no aspiration, yet there is neither doing nor non-doing."
"Great King, if there were anything to be established or performed as a practice, then the actions of body, speech, and mind would constitute what is done. However,
if there were nothing to be done and no practice to be performed, such that one produced nothing through body, speech, and mind, then there would be no 'doing'."
"Therefore, Great King!
All dharmas are entirely without marks; that which has no activity and nothingness is precisely their mark.
He then asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is it to practice while having nothing to practice, to neither create nor not create, and to neither increase nor decrease?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"If one is able to not dwell on the past as already exhausted, not dwell on the future as yet unarrived, and not dwell on the present so that nothing arises; if one does not conceive of permanence or impermanence—this is to have neither practice nor non-practice. To be able to equate form with all causes and conditions, such that for these manifold conditions there is neither increase nor decrease."
He asked Niu-shou again:
"Are the desires of worldly affliction this very path?
How do they accord with it?"
Niu-shou replied:
"What do you think, O King?
Does that which is called 'light' unite with darkness?"
He replied: "No.
When the sun rises, all darkness is extinguished."
“Does Your Majesty know where darkness goes when it departs?
In which direction does it reside, and in what place does it accumulate?
He replied:
"It does not reach it.
Rumaśir said, "So it is, Great King!"

When one gives rise to the wisdom of the Path, worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished; yet one does not know the place where these afflictions converge, for they have no location and no direction. For this reason, one should understand that the Path and worldly afflictions do not coalesce, and moreover, that which is equal to worldly afflictions is called the Path.
That which is equal to the Path, afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise equal; afflictions and the Path are equal without distinction, and all phenomena (*dharma*) are also thus equal.
If one makes such a conceptual analysis, then afflictions are the Path.
Why is this so? It is because of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that the Way appears!
Afflictions have no form and possess nothing; therefore, the one who seeks afflictions is the Way itself.
The King asked again:
"How can one seek the Way within the afflictions?
Niu-shou replied:
"Even if there is something sought, it does not transcend the human mind, nor does one think to say, 'This is affliction (kleśa), and this is the Way.
For this reason, affliction is the Way, and those who possess affliction likewise enter the Way."
The king asked again:
"How do the afflictions enter the Way?
What constitutes their practice?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"To have no practice regarding any phenomena is the practice of the Way;
likewise, to have no non-practice regarding any phenomena is the practice of the Way."
The King asked again:
"Practicing the Way in such a manner—what is its ultimate destination?
Niu-shou replied:
"One who practices in this way has no destination.
The King asked again,
"Does the Path not lead to Nirvana?"
Niu-shou asked, "Are there any dharmas that reach extinction?
He replied:
"No," said Niu-shou. "For this reason, Great King!"
"To reach the state of non-attainment is the path of the worthy and holy.
He asked again:
"Where do those who are worthy and holy abide?"
Niu-shou said:
"The path of the worthy sages abides nowhere.
He asked again:
"Does that noble and holy path not abide in the precepts, extensive learning, concentration, and wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"The precepts of the noble ones are characterized by the absence of any mark of practice; the holy state of meditative concentration is characterized by the absence of heedlessness."
The characteristic of non-attachment is the noble concentration;
the characteristic of non-conceptualization is the noble wisdom.
What do you think, O King?
"If there is no activity and no negligence,
is there any place of abiding? He replied, "No."
Niu-shou said:
"For this reason, Your Majesty should know that the path of the worthy and the sages is that which abides nowhere.
The King asked again:
“Noble son, noble daughter, how does one turn toward the Way?
Mañjuśrī replied:

“If, in that which is sought, one does not perceive any phenomena as being permanent or impermanent, nor does one obtain anything; if one does not reckon any phenomena as being pure or impure, empty or non-empty, self or non-self, suffering or pleasure;”

Regarding all phenomena, there is likewise nothing to be apprehended; not perceiving any phenomenon as existing at the beginning or the end, or as being in a state of parinirvāṇa—one who practices in this manner is proceeding toward the Path.
King Ajātaśatru addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

"For this reason, you should indeed accept my invitation; by means of this, may I be freed from all inversions and attain liberation through pure conduct free from conceptual discrimination. Together with your retinue, please come to the palace for a meal."
Niu-shou said:
"As previously explained, all things are utterly non-existent; there is no one who gives birth to them, nor is there such a thing as 'good' or 'not good'!"
That which is non-existent has no liberation; that which is liberated is itself non-existent, such that there is neither liberation nor one who is liberated. Why is this so?
"All dharmas are naturally pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Mañjuśrī:
"Accept King Ajātaśatru’s invitation; by this cause and condition, enable countless people to attain beneficial benefit and reach the peace of liberation."
When the youth Mañjuśrī saw that the World-Honored One had exhorted him, he said:
“Yes, sir; I shall accept this invitation, for I dare not disobey or fail the teaching of the Tathāgata.”

King Ajātaśatru was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; having seen that his invitation had been accepted, a virtuous mind arose within him. He prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, as well as at those of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and the entire assembly of noble ones, and then withdrew to invite Śāriputra, asking:
"How many people are there in Mañjuśrī’s retinue?"
Śāriputra replied, "We shall go together with five hundred people.

When the king entered the city and returned to his palace, that very night he prepared various foods of a hundred flavors and provided five hundred couches, upon which he spread countless seats. He adorned the palace with hanging silk banners and canopies, burned various famous incenses, and scattered many flowers. Furthermore, throughout the four crossroads and everywhere within and outside the city, all was swept clean and sprinkled with fragrant liquid. He ordered the men and women, the old and young of the kingdom’s people, to adorn themselves in magnificent attire and carry incense and flowers, so that they might all together pay homage to the youthful Mañjuśrī.
Chapter Six: On Dhāraṇī (Middle). Chapter Six, "On Dhāraṇī. At that time, during the first watch of the night, Mañjuśrī emerged from his chamber and reflected to himself:
"It is not appropriate for me to attend the King's invitation accompanied by only a small retinue."

Now I shall go to other Buddha-lands to invite all the bodhisattvas, so that they may everywhere hear the exposition of the Dharma and sever all their doubts, and then partake of a meal at the palace of King Ajātaśatru.

The youth Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta, like a valiant warrior extending or contracting his arm, suddenly vanished. In an instant, he transcended eighty thousand Buddha-fields and arrived at the eastern realm called Constant Renown, where the Buddha named Vigataśravaṇaśiras Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently resides and teaches the Dharma, preaching the scriptures of purity for the sake of all bodhisattvas.

In that Buddha-world, the Tathāgata at one time equally turns the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) to their ultimate limit; he naturally attains mastery therein and fully proclaims the Dharma of non-retrogression.

In that Buddha-land, all the various trees are laden with diverse flowers and abundant fruits; from these trees there constantly and spontaneously issue forth the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the voices of the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the irreversible wheel. For this reason, the world is named Constant Renown.
The precious sound of this Way is never interrupted; therefore, it is called "Ever-Famed.
Ju-shou (Ratnamati), a youthful bodhisattva, went to the abode of the Buddha Vimuktarutaśiras, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Tathāgata:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
He dispatched various bodhisattvas to go with me to the Sahā world, to visit King Ajātaśatru’s palace and accept his invitation.
When the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna had finished speaking, he addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“O sons of noble family!
"Go together with Ruci to the Sahā world, according to your wish.
Thereupon, twenty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the assembly simultaneously raised their voices and replied:
"Yes, World-Honored One!"
"We wish to go with Mañjuśrī to the Sahā world.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with twenty-two thousand bodhisattvas, suddenly vanished from the country of Constant Renown and arrived at the Sahā world, where he entered his own chamber.
Rushou gathered the various bodhisattva mahāsattvas and, during the first watch of the night, preached the Dharma of dhāraṇī.
"What is meant by dhāraṇī?
It is that which, as a dhāraṇī, governs and unifies all dharmas into one."
First, his mind never forgot [the goal].
Second, wherever he went, he was never distracted.
Third, his mind never experienced a moment of abandonment or neglect. Fourth.
Fifth, training in the activity of wisdom;
sixth, thoroughly investigating the definitive meaning of all phenomena;
seventh, discerning with correct wisdom.
8. That those who attain the realization of the fruits are merely words;
9. That they ferry others across to the state of profound stillness;
10. That they set forth in systematic order all dharmas, chapters, and phrases.
1. To grasp the essentials of the worthy and holy ones;
2. Not to sever the Buddha’s teachings;
3. Not to contravene the laws and regulations.
Fourth, to embrace the assembly of all worthy and noble ones;
fifth, [to master] the various divisions and scriptures of the sūtra teachings;
sixth, to enter into all supreme and extraordinary wisdoms.
7. Not being attached to the assembly and not being timid;
8. Walking through the assembly and proclaiming the sūtras without fear or hesitation;
9. Producing the voices of the devas and possessing discerning wisdom.
Twenty: He probes and articulates his voice for the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, preaching the Dharma for them.
First, they produce the melodic voices of Śakra and Brahmā;
second, they awaken to and realize impartiality and correctness, knowing the origins of all faculties;
third, they discern and refine false views regarding all established positions.
Fourth, through dhāraṇī, one observes the fundamental dispositions and destinies of all sentient beings;
fifth, one maintains an impartial mind toward those with whom one dwells;
sixth, one remains unshaken by the eight worldly concerns.
7. To be fully endowed with all truly correct dharmas;
8. To preach the Dharma according to the retributive fruits and realizations of their respective transgressions and merits;
9. To inspire and initiate the volitional activities and undertakings of sentient beings.
1. Establishing all the multitudes in the place of the precepts; 2.
His wisdom universally entering into oneness; 3.
Acting as a substitute for the masses to bear their heavy burdens.
3. Not to feel weariness or aversion despite diligent exertion;
4. To understand that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure;
5. To expound this inherent purity for the sake of others.
Sixth, to explain the meaning of the Dharma through primordial pure wisdom;
seventh, to possess unimpeded wisdom;
eighth, to practice the giving of the Dharma.
9. His mind is firm and never weary.
40. Whatever he speaks is free from doubt or entanglement.
1. He does not crave any offerings or material gain.
2. Not forgetting or abandoning the mind of all-encompassing wisdom;
3. Diligently accumulating the foundations of various practices with tranquility;
4. Giving without weariness and constantly encouraging others toward all-encompassing wisdom.
5. To never tire of observing the precepts in order to exhort and transform all sentient beings;
6. To never tire of practicing patience in order to seek the physical form of a Buddha;
7. To never tire of practicing diligence in order to accumulate the roots of all virtues.
8. To practice with single-minded diligence and tireless devotion so as to eliminate all darkness;
9. To enter into all practices with tireless wisdom;
10. To cultivate the karmic deeds of the Way and Dharma within all these things so that nothing arises.
"O sons of noble family!

That which is called 'dhāraṇī' encompasses all the essential meanings of inconceivable dharmas; because it maintains all dharmas as being without activity and without non-activity, it is called 'dhāraṇī'."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
That which is dhāraṇī maintains and upholds all dharmas.
What is meant by 'dhāraṇī of all dharmas'? "
Grasping at all phenomena as entirely empty, grasping at all phenomena as entirely without conceptualization, and grasping at all phenomena as entirely without aspiration;
detached from all modes of activity, quiescent and formless;
altogether non-existent and without anything to be perceived.
It neither has any activity nor any location;
it neither arises nor originates;
it neither proceeds toward anything nor undergoes cessation.
There is no coming and no going, nor is there any destruction;
there is nothing to be crossed over and nothing to be defeated;
there is neither purity nor impurity.
There is neither adornment nor non-adornment;
neither attachment nor possession;
neither seeing nor hearing.
There is neither anything forgotten nor anything taught;
there is neither outflow nor conceptualization;
there is neither departure from thought nor correspondence or non-correspondence; there is neither inversion nor fulfillment.
There is no self, no person, no life-span, and no vital principle;

there is neither negligence nor anything received, neither anything grasped nor anything extraordinary. It is like space, having no name or renown, nothing to be acquired and nothing to be destroyed, and being without duality.
Thoroughly abiding at the fundamental limit, all dharma-realms and all dharmas abide in the absence of a foundation.
This is called dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, son of good family!
All dharmas are like illusions and are entirely spontaneous.

One who upholds all dharmas [realizes they are] spontaneous like a dream, spontaneous like a mirage, spontaneous like a shadow, spontaneous like an echo, spontaneous like a transformation, spontaneous like foam, spontaneous like a bubble, and spontaneous like space.
"To discern all phenomena in this manner is called dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said:
"For example, son of good family!"
That which the earth bears encompasses all things without exception; it neither increases nor decreases, nor does it set anything aside, nor does it grow weary of it.

Likewise, if a bodhisattva attains *dhāraṇī*, they are able to benefit all sentient beings, bestowing grace and providing salvation for incalculable eons. From the root of all virtues up to the attainment of universal wisdom, they maintain and sustain them with their mind, yet they do not set anything aside, nor do they grow weary of it.
“O son of good family!
For example, upon this earth, all sentient beings depend on it for their livelihood; whether they have two legs or four, there is none to whom it does not respond.”
It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has attained dhāraṇī; they bring great benefit to the multitude of living beings.
"For example, son of good family!"
Herbs, trees, the hundred grains, and all manner of fruits all grow because of the earth.
Even so, if a bodhisattva attains dhāraṇī, they are likewise able to give rise to and propagate all the roots of virtue and the teachings of the Buddhas.
“Just as, son of good family!
That which the earth supports has no place of its own to rest upon; it neither grieves nor is distressed; it does not move or shake, nor does it increase or decrease.
In this way, the bodhisattva likewise has nothing to place; he does not feel sorrow or distress, neither increasing nor decreasing, and remains unshakable.
"For example, son of good family!

Just as this earth receives all the rain from heaven without ever becoming weary, so too the Bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* receives all the scriptures of the Buddhas, as well as all the teachings of the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; furthermore, when those of right view, practitioners of equanimity, śramaṇas, brahmins, and all sentient beings—whether in the heavens or the world below—hear his preaching of the Dharma, they never grow weary, nor do they become fatigued by listening to the sūtras he expounds.

“Just as, noble son! Whatever is sown in the earth all grows according to the season without missing its proper time, nor does it grow out of order, but flourishes in accordance with the appropriate timing.”

When a bodhisattva has thus attained this dhāraṇī, they encompass all dharmas of merit; they do not deceive others, nor do they miss the proper time. Fully endowed with their practice, they sit beneath the Bodhi tree and, remaining at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they reach all-encompassing wisdom.
“Just as, noble son!
A courageous and eminent gentleman who enters into battle within his realm subdues his enemies, and there are none who do not submit to him.
A bodhisattva who has thus attained this dhāraṇī dwells at the site of enlightenment, sits beneath the Bodhi tree, and subdues all Māras.
"For example, son of noble family!..."

One examines all phenomena to see whether they are permanent or impermanent; if they are subtle, one considers them as peaceful and non-self, and likewise reckons them as impermanent, defiled, suffering, and non-self.
Why is this so? O son of good family!
Because one has already departed from duality, it is called dhāraṇī.
“Just as, noble son, space does not fail to sustain anything,
yet it is neither a dhāraṇī nor is there anything it does not sustain; so too,
the bodhisattva who has attained such a dhāraṇī gathers and encompasses the essentials of all phenomena.”
“O son of good family!
For example, all dharmas and all false views are entirely empty, and [the Bodhisattva] maintains them all through total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
A Bodhisattva who thus attains such total retention grasps nothing that is not encompassed.”
The dhāraṇī is thus: it encompasses and protects the meaning of all dharmas.
Therefore, son of good family, one should know that the dhāraṇī is inexhaustible.
When there is no exhaustion, there is no negligence;
when there is no negligence, one dwells in the middle.
One who dwells in equanimity has no body; thus, the realm of space is already like empty space, and space and earth are then non-dual.
When the youth Mañjuśrī spoke these words, five hundred bodhisattvas attained this dhāraṇī. Chapter Seven:

The Three Baskets (Middle). In the seventh chapter, "The Three Baskets," at midnight, the youth Mañjuśrī expounded for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas the secret scripture of the bodhisattvas known as the *Tripiṭaka*.
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s casket of essential secrets?
All the teachings of the various sūtras enter into this casket without exception—
whether they be worldly dharmas or world-transcending dharmas, conditioned dharmas or unconditioned dharmas."

Whether they be wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, blameworthy or blameless dharmas, outflowing or non-outflowing dharmas, they all come to converge and enter into the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Why is this so?
The essential contents of the Bodhisattva’s scriptural treasury consist in understanding the meaning of all dharmas.
For example, son of good family!

Suppose this trichiliocosm—with its ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion earths, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Sumeru kings of mountains, and ten billion great oceans—were all rolled up and condensed into a single Buddha-field within this trichiliocosm.
In this way, son of good family!
Whether it be the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of those in training;
or the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
If the dharmas of bodhisattvas and the dharmas of buddhas all enter and take refuge in the bodhisattva’s casket, why is this?
Because the bodhisattva’s casket encompasses and protects all, nurturing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas within the Mahāyāna.
For example, son of good family!
When the roots and trunk of a tree are firm and flourishing, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will grow lush and abundant.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If one embraces the Bodhisattva-treasury, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thereby embraces all vehicles and nurtures the dharmas of all qualities.

The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is called the "Infinite Vessel. It is named the Infinite Vessel because, for example, it is like the great ocean which receives immeasurable water, serving as a container that cannot be calculated in its true capacity.

All the nāgas, ghosts, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other classes of sentient beings, including those among the birds and beasts—[the Tathāgata] contains and receives all such as these as an infinite vessel.

The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is likewise the essential secret of the sūtras; it serves as a vessel for infinite giving, hearing, ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. For this reason, it is called the "Casket of the Bodhisattvas."
For example, just as those blood-bearing creatures born in the great ocean do not drink any other water because they were born there, but consume only the ocean water;

so too, the bodhisattva who practices the Bodhisattva-piṭaka does not perform any practice in other dharmas, but constantly cultivates the meaning of all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms. For this reason, it is called the "Casket of the Bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva possesses these three essential treasuries.
What are the three?
The first is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; the second is called the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka; and the third is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
As for the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, one attains liberation by relying on the sounds of others.
The Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka is that which clearly understands the twelve links of dependent origination and discerns the exhaustion of the causes and conditions from which retribution arises.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which comprehensively organizes the correct principles of immeasurable dharmas and awakens through individual discernment.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Śrāvaka vehicle possesses no Tripiṭaka, nor does the Pratyekabuddha possess such a collection. It is the Bodhisattvas who thoroughly study and refine the secret essentials of the Tripiṭaka; it is through the Bodhisattva-dharma that the Tripiṭaka arises—namely, for the sake of the Śrāvakas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Unsurpassed Right and True Way—and therefore it is called the 'Tripiṭaka'."

The Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to exhort and transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in the three vehicles—namely, the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment; for this reason, the Bodhisattva is called the Tripitaka.
There are these three piṭakas and no other collections of study.
What are the three?
They are the study of the śrāvakas, the study of the pratyekabuddhas, and the study of the bodhisattvas.
What is meant by the training of the śrāvaka?
It is that which can only illuminate the characteristics of one's own conduct.
The training of the pratyekabuddha is called the intermediate training.
Practicing great compassion refers to the training of a bodhisattva, culminating in immeasurable wisdom and encompassing great pity.
Those who are śrāvakas neither train in nor understand what is to be learned by pratyekabuddhas;
those who are pratyekabuddhas neither train in nor understand what is to be learned by bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva studies all that which the śrāvakas follow and learn; he thoroughly understands them but does not take pleasure in them, nor does he encourage others to practice those deeds.
He studies all that which the pratyekabuddhas follow and learn; he thoroughly understands them but does not take pleasure in them, nor does he exhort or transform others to cultivate their vehicle.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva who trains in that which a bodhisattva ought to learn fully understands it all; they joyfully aspire to and exhort others to practice the conduct of that vehicle. Having exhorted them to such practice, they then explain the liberation practiced by śrāvakas, also discourse upon the liberation practiced by pratyekabuddhas, and analyze the liberation followed by bodhisattvas.
Thus it is, son of good family!

Whoever thoroughly understands this which is to be learned is called the "Casket of the Bodhisattva. Just as whatever is contained within a vessel of lapis lazuli appears at that very moment with its natural nature manifesting as the color of lapis lazuli, so it is here.
"In this way, son of good family!
Even if a bodhisattva enters the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and dwells among all phenomena, they perceive all phenomena as being entirely the Buddha-dharma."

Even if a bodhisattva enters the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they do not perceive any location for all dharmas; even if they should attain realization of the Buddha-vehicle, they do not see any semblance or likeness of all dharmas. Those who do not train in the bodhisattva training, however, perceive all dharmas as having a location.
If one studies what is to be studied by a bodhisattva, they do not perceive any phenomena as having a location;

if one studies what is to be studied by a bodhisattva, they do not perceive any phenomena as having a place of abiding, for they do not practice with the calculation that all these things are merely spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
In this way, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva enters the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, then in whatever practices they engage and whatever dharmas they traverse, they will see all of them as the dharmas of the Buddhas.

If a bodhisattva enters the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and does not perceive any semblance or likeness among all phenomena, and even if they thoroughly understand the teachings of the Buddhas, they likewise do not behold any locus of phenomena.

In training in the bodhisattva training, one does not perceive any destination to which phenomena tend; yet for one who does not cultivate contemplation, all phenomena are seen as having both opposition and conformity.
When all sentient beings perceive things as being contrary [to the Dharma], the Bodhisattva perceives all phenomena as being in accord with the correct [Dharma].
Regarding all phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon that is not the Buddha-Dharma; for this reason, it is called the "Treasury" (kośa) of the Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family! The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is of unfathomable depth;

the words it expounds are timely and immeasurable. Its established positions are inconceivable, and it radiates light that penetrates everywhere. It is boundless, illuminating all without exception, bringing great benefit and causing all to take refuge therein. Through its various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, it causes all sentient beings to delight in the rootless."
If those who are in training, those who have already trained, and those who are just about to train were all to enter this Bodhisattva Casket, they would then reach the Great Vehicle.
"Those who have already desired to study, those who are currently about to attain it, and those who have not yet arrived—may they all reach their goal and enter [the path] universally.

Thus, at midnight, Ruciraketu, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas, expounded the secret essentials of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka sūtra, extensively analyzing and elucidating its principles and the destination to which they lead.

Chapter Eight: The Non-Retrogression Wheel (Middle Section). During the final watch of the night, the Youthful Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta again extensively proclaimed and expounded for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas the adamantine traces of the words of the Non-Retrogression Wheel.
"What is called the 'Wheel of Non-Retrogression'?
Furthermore, son of good family!

As for why it is named the Wheel of Non-Retrogression: when a bodhisattva now preaches the Dharma, all who come to listen attain the ultimate refuge and do not turn back; thus he expounds the Wheel of Non-Retrogression so that they may find faith and joy."
A bodhisattva practitioner who has attained the wheel of non-retrogression does not perform various practices for the sake of sentient beings;
does not cultivate various practices for the sake of all dharmas;
and does not initiate various practices within various lands.
They do not engage in diverse practices toward the various Buddhas;
they do not engage in diverse practices toward the various vehicles.

They universally perceive all that is reached, turning the wheel of Dharma without destroying the dharma-realm; this is called turning the wheel of Dharma, and for this reason it is named the non-retrogressive wheel.
That which he turns is without interruption;
its turning is consistent and without a second wheel;
that wheel is thus like the wheel of compassion.
The natural principle of where that wheel proceeds lies within one's own reach;
the sphere where that wheel proceeds is the wheel of the Dharma-realm field.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva has faith and delight in this wheel of non-retrogression, they will attain liberation from the afflictions of their own body; they will then have faith and delight in all that is worthy of faith and all that is conceived, and they will likewise believe in everything that the Tathāgata brings forth, attaining liberation through such faith.

Regarding the Tathāgata, there is no duality of liberation, nor does he speak of duality. Just as the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Tathāgata are liberation, so too are the marks of all phenomena and the conceptualizations of all phenomena. To have faith in the liberation of the Tathāgata is to be without conceptualization; having already departed from the marks of liberation, one reaches spontaneity (*svayambhū*) for oneself. No practice can surpass this, nor can any wisdom exceed it; therefore, it is called the "Wheel of Non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The non-retrogressive wheel does not retrogress from form, because form is naturally so;
it is likewise with sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Consciousness does not retrogress, because consciousness is naturally so."
Why is this? Because it is non-retrogressive regarding all dharmas;
being like that which has no origin, it constitutes the Wheel of Dharma. For this reason, it is called the Non-Retrogressive Wheel.
That wheel of Dharma has no boundaries; it has no dimensions, no corners, and no interruption, because it is not a revolving wheel.
That wheel of Dharma also has no gate, because there is no duality; thus, it is the gate of the wheel of Dharma.
That wheel of Dharma has no one who can turn it, because there is nothing to be turned.
That wheel of Dharma is also without anything spoken, for the wheel of Dharma is beyond speech;
that wheel of Dharma is also without name or renown and without manifestation, for the wheel has nothing to be acquired;
furthermore, one should reckon this non-retrogressive wheel as entering into emptiness, for it has no characteristics of wandering.
The Gate of Serene Detachment is so called because it has no characteristic of coming;
it reaches everywhere because it has the characteristic of emptiness;
all things are equally governed by their original purity and signlessness—therefore, it is named the Non-retrogressive Wheel.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Because the wheel of non-retrogression travels and reaches its destination, it is called the 'wheel of non-retrogression.
Because it relinquishes all things and proceeds directly to its destination, it is called the 'wheel of non-retrogression.'"
Thus, Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Furthermore, noble sons!
That which is called the 'adamantine trace' (vajrapada) is because all dharmas are entirely extinguished and quiescent."
What is meant by the cessation and tranquility of all dharmas?
Furthermore, son of good family!
One who has realized emptiness possesses the adamantine traces, for they have eliminated all sixty-two types of false doubts.
That which is signless (*animitta*) is the vajra-track, because it severs all conceptualizations;
that which is wishless (*apraṇihita*) is the vajra-track, because it brings all conditioned existence within the five destinies to cessation and quiescence;
that which is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the vajra-track, because it transcends all various boundaries.
That which is without basis is the vajra trace, because it brings about the cessation and tranquility of non-self;
that which is free from form and desire is the vajra trace, because it eliminates all that consists of craving and attachment;
that which proceeds by way of dependent origination is the vajra trace, because it does not destroy the fundamental nature.
"To investigate non-action is the trace of the Vajra-sentence, for it perceives that all dharmas are spontaneous.

Thus did the youth Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta extensively analyze the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas throughout three nights. All those bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of the Proximate Radiant Flower;

when a bodhisattva achieves this concentration, a hundred thousand rays of light are emitted from each and every pore, and within each ray of light, the forms and countenances of a hundred thousand Buddhas are manifested through transformation.

Furthermore, wherever these Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, reside within their respective Buddha-fields, they manifest the performance of Buddha-works to guide and instruct sentient beings; all classes of living beings welcome and receive them, listening to and accepting their Dharma teachings.
Chapter Nine: On Transformation (Middle). At that time, King Ajātaśatru rose early at dawn and went to where Mañjuśrī was, prostrating himself and saying:
"The offerings have been prepared; the time has come for you to depart."
The venerable Mahākāśyapa rose early at dawn, donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and set out with five hundred bhikṣus to enter the great city of Śrāvastī for alms. On the way, he thought:
"It is still too early for me to go on my almsround; I should instead go to see the youth Mañjuśrī."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went there and engaged in extensive conversation with Rāśtrapāla, discoursing upon the firm essentials.
Rāśtrapāla then said to him:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!..."
"Where are you headed this morning? He replied,
"I have come to seek instruction because I wish to go out for alms."
Mañjuśrī said, "Now you and your retinue should come to where I have prepared the meal; I shall share with you the requisites for alms-gathering.
Kāśyapa replied:
"The requisites have already arrived; I have come here for the sake of the Dharma, not for food.
He further said, "Kāśyapa!..."
"I shall indeed accept your invitation.

Regarding the two matters of receiving offerings—namely, the great Dharma offering and the meal of food and drink—I shall speak without ceasing the Dharma, yet I shall not fail to partake of the food.
Kāśyapa replied:
"Because we have undertaken the practice of the Dharma, we have ceased eating and do not consume food, dedicating our entire life to the Dharma until the end of our existence.
Why is this? It is because one can only attain it by not following others."
"This Dharma-gate is indeed consistent with the correct principle as spoken by you, O Benevolent One.
He asked again:
"Now, Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas—what do they eat?"
Niu-shou replied:
"That which we eat and that which we bestow neither increases nor diminishes;
it does not move within saṃsāra, nor does it approach nirvāṇa."
Nor does one transcend the stage of ordinary beings, nor does one realize the dharma of the noble ones;
one does not bypass the śrāvakas, nor does one abandon the pratyekabuddhas.

We shall now explain what was requested: as for that giving, it neither purifies wisdom nor the objects of cognition; it neither diminishes nor increases, yet it does not lead to liberation; regarding all sūtras and dharmas, there is nothing produced, nor is any dharma attained, nor is anything explained.
Kāśyapa replied, “This is the great and boundless generosity of extensive giving; it is brought about by having entered into the state of non-origination.
At that time, Rāhula thought to himself:
"Entering the city today, it would be fitting to manifest transformations like those of a Buddha.
At that moment, he entered the meditative absorption known as the *sarva-devarddhi-vikurvaṇa-samādhi*.

When he entered this samādhi as his formal meditative attainment, immediately the entire trichiliocosm became level and even throughout, like the palm of a hand. A great radiance pervaded this entire Buddha-field without exception. Those in the hells who were suffering in torment found immediate relief; those among animals and hungry ghosts who were distressed instantly attained peace and security; and the minds of all classes of sentient beings were fully opened and liberated.

Free from lust, anger, and delusion; without stinginess or envy, and likewise without flattery or deceit; free from the fetters of malice and arrogance; there is nothing that arises, nor is there any burning affliction.
At that time, sentient beings looked upon one another as they would a father or a mother.
Beholding this trichiliocosm shaking in six ways, the devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm all assembled and made offerings to Puṣya!
With hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, stringed songs, and performing arts, celestial flowers rained down to adorn and prepare the roads.

As the youth Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta entered this samādhi, from his residence to the city gates, the roads became naturally adorned, level, broad, and long. Countless treasures of the seven jewels appeared spontaneously as various decorations; immeasurable jewels transformed into jeweled moats, within which lotuses, water lilies, and *heng* flowers grew in full, brilliant splendor. Above the moats, jeweled canopies with hanging pearls were magically created, along with banners, streamers, and flower parasols. Surrounding the moats on all sides were railings, and to the left and right of these railings stood jewel trees, exceedingly tall and great, with various jeweled cords interlacing and connecting them one after another.
Beside each jeweled tree there was a jeweled rack upon which incense burners were placed, all burning various famous incenses;
the fragrance from each incense burner wafted for forty *li*.

Between the trees were manifested jeweled bathing pools, filled with water of eight flavors; the bottom of each pool was entirely of golden sand, and they were encircled by jeweled railings with lapis lazuli cliffs, where blue lotuses, water lilies, and *henghua* flowers grew in abundance.
Beneath the various jewel trees, the ground was made of jewels; upon all these jeweled grounds, rows of precious incense vases were set out, burning famous fragrances.
Under each and every jewel tree, five hundred jade maidens stood solemnly in formation, each establishing the virtue of giving.

Through this concentration, Ārya Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the samādhi of right reception manifested itself immediately; for the sake of those teachers of heterodox paths and outsiders, he displayed transformations so sublime and immeasurable that there was nowhere they did not pervade.
The youthful Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, took up his bowl, and, intending to depart, said to Kāśyapa:
"O Mahākāśyapa!..."
"You should therefore go before me, while I follow behind. Why is this?
Venerable Mahākāśyapa is of advanced age;

you have long cultivated the holy life as a śramaṇa and have not yet gone forth to study under the Tathāgata. Considering all the arhats in the world, they have all received instruction from you. For this reason, it is fitting that you go before me, while I remain behind."
Kāśyapa replied:

"According to the laws and principles, one is not made venerable by years; rather, it is wisdom as recorded in the laws and principles that constitutes venerability. Only one who possesses divine intelligence and saintly attainment may be considered venerable;
only one who is widely learned and possesses eloquence is said to be venerable."
One whose faculties are clear and penetrating is called "venerable," and according to what is recorded in the laws and teachings, it is by this that one is deemed venerable.

Judging by this, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta possesses towering wisdom, vast learning, universal attainment, and unimpeded eloquence; he understands the fundamental nature of all sentient beings. For these reasons, he is the most preeminent and far-reaching; you, O Benevolent One, are the Great Venerable and should stand at the front, while I should remain behind. Now, I wish to employ a metaphor to distinguish this meaning.
Kāśyapa spoke again:

"It is like the cub of a lion that has been born not long ago; though it is young and its physical strength is not yet fully developed, wherever that lion cub strides and wherever its breath flows, all the wild deer and various beasts, hearing its fierce spirit, flee in every direction."

Suppose there is a great elephant with six tusks, sixty years of age and of immense stature; if it were bound three times with leather thongs, upon smelling the fierce and majestic scent of a lion cub, it would become terrified and anxious, leaping and struggling with all its might, snapping the triple bonds and charging away, entering among the mountains, valleys, streams, forests, thickets, crags, and trees, or plunging into great waters to drown itself.

Where birds nest in the branches of trees and wild beasts hide and flee into their lairs, where water-dwelling fish and turtles retreat to the depths of the abyss, and where all flying birds soar through the void—so too it is with the bodhisattva who has first resolved his mind.

Even if the power of wisdom of one who has resolved his mind has not yet fully matured or been perfected, his mind still aspires with lofty pride and practices the lion’s stride; he transcends the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and within the palaces of all the māras, he harbors fear and cannot find peace of mind.

Suppose a lion cub sees another lion’s majestic power and fierce momentum, and when that lion roars, the cub hears its sound without fear or terror; it feels no anxiety and has nothing to dread, but instead leaps for joy with its fur bristling and sleek, and mounting upon that power and momentum, it too shall let out a roar.

When the Mahāsattva Śāriputra heard this lion’s roar of the Buddha, he was neither alarmed nor terrified, nor did he harbor any fear or apprehension; instead, he felt no dread or difficulty, but was filled with joy and leaped for gladness as a sense of peace arose within him, thinking: "I, too, shall practice in this way, just like the lion’s roar of the present Buddha."

Suppose there were someone who said that while the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas represent impartiality and true correctness, the Tathāgata is the most honored, yet the Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind [for enlightenment] is the very root; these words would be ultimate sincerity, impartiality, and freedom from error.

Why is this so? Because from him all dharmas are born and universally manifested; therefore, it is clearly known that Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī) is the Honored One. Although he is young in years, he is the elder among sages; he ought to go before, and I shall follow behind.
The youth Mañjuśrī went at the head, followed by the bodhisattvas, and the assembly of śrāvakas followed in their wake.

As Mañjuśrī proceeded along the magnificently adorned jeweled path, celestial flowers rained down, countless musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, the earth shook in six ways at that moment, and a great radiance shone forth everywhere, penetrating all things.

At that time, the transformations and majestic spiritual power manifested by Mañjuśrī caused great wonder; he emitted a great radiance and rained down fragrant flowers, while the sounds of various musical instruments resonated in harmony as they entered the city of Rājagṛha.
King Ajātaśatru reflected:

"When Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), together with twenty-three thousand bodhisattvas and surrounded by his retinue of śrāvakas, sets out on the road, I already feel fear; now that I have prepared offerings for five hundred people, these arrivals are so numerous—how can I provide for them all, and where will they sit?"
"With what shall I feed him?
He then thought to himself:
"Does the youth Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta harbor doubts or errors regarding the marks of fruition that he has given rise to this thought?"

At that moment, established by the majestic power and holy virtue of Mañjuśrī, the Celestial King Śāntamati immediately transformed himself into the spirit Kinki, assuming a subtle and wondrous form, and addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Great King, please stop; do not worry, and do not trouble yourself with anxiety."

Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), the Youthful Truth, possesses the boundless wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). He manifests great merit with majestic and brilliant spiritual power; his divine might is vast and his auspicious radiance is magnificent as he arrives upon the path. With a single meal, he is able to provide for the entire trichiliocosm, causing all classes of sentient beings to be fully satisfied; how much more so for these twenty-three thousand followers who have come?
For this reason, there is no need for further anxiety.
Your Majesty, please remain at ease and do not provide further offerings; all who come shall be fully satisfied. Why is this so?
"Noble Head (Ruci) bestows great bounty; he has attained inexhaustible merit, and his manifold blessings are immeasurable.
King Ajātaśatru, at that moment, leaped for joy beyond self-mastery, regarding Noble Head with a vast intention as if he were the World-Honored Buddha.

King Ajātaśatru, together with his various ministers, palace officials, and attendants, brought flowers, incense, blended perfumes, garments, banners, streamers, canopies, and musical instruments such as lutes, harps, and *konghou* zithers to welcome Mañjuśrī. Having prostrated themselves in worship, they escorted Mañjuśrī into the city and back to the palace.
When Niu-shou (Sudhana) and his retinue first entered the city, the common people within the city each brought whatever they possessed to offer as alms.
At that time, within the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Puguang (Universal Observation).
Niu-shou said:
"O son of noble family!
Let this palace accommodate those who have gathered."

Immediately following these instructions, he examined his surroundings and surveyed the entire palace of Ajātaśatru; it was naturally vast and spacious, adorned with suspended silk streamers, flower canopies, and standing banners and pennants, while its level ground was broad and strewn with various fragrant flowers.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmotkṣepa.
Mañjuśrī addressed him, saying:
"O son of noble family!..."
"Prepare the seats for the assembly.

At that moment, having received these instructions, he raised his hand and snapped his fingers; thereupon, twenty-three thousand couches and seats were spontaneously provided within that palace hall, adorned with various exquisite ornaments and subtle decorations. Countless cushions and mats were spread upon them, and the youth Mañjuśrī, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas, all took their seats together, followed by the śrāvakas.
When the King saw that Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī) and the various bodhisattvas and śrāvakas had finished sitting, he came forward and addressed him:
"Please wait a moment while I prepare further offerings. Niu-shou replied:
"May the Great King rest at ease; you need not trouble yourself, for we shall provide all that is necessary.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues, all came to attend upon and serve the youth Mañjuśrī. Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of Devas, the Lady Bhadra, and countless thousands of other celestial maidens brought celestial sandalwood, various incenses, honey-scented incense, and powdered incense, scattering them as offerings before all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
At that time, although the bodhisattvas saw various flower fragrances and celestial maidens, they had no perception of celestial maidens and no perception of flower fragrances.

A Brahmā from the realm of Akaniṣṭha manifested in the form of a brahmin student (*māṇava*), holding a fly-whisk in his hand and standing as an attendant on the left side of Mañjuśrī, fanning him with the whisk;
each of the Brahmā sons likewise held fly-whisks and stood as attendants to the bodhisattvas, fanning them.

The Dragon King Wu-chen (Unconfused) does not manifest his physical form, but remains in the void, suspending strings of pearls from which flow water of eight flavors—cool, refreshing, and delicious—to provide for all needs.
Before each of the bodhisattvas and all the śrāvakas, there are likewise suspended strings of pearls that emit this exquisite water to supply their requirements.
King Ajātaśatru thought to himself:
"These bodhisattvas do not carry alms bowls;
where will they eat?"
Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), knowing the king’s thoughts, addressed him, saying:
“These noble beings travel to wherever they go without carrying alms bowls. Whenever they visit the various Buddha-lands and sit down intending to eat, the bowls arrive of their own accord.”
"This was established by these bodhisattvas from the beginning, and furthermore, it is due to the vows formerly made by that Tathāgata; thus the bowl has come from space and rests in his palm.
King Ajātaśatru asked Mañjuśrī, "From which buddha-field have these bodhisattvas come?"
"What is the name of this world?
By what title is the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, known? Mañjuśrī replied:
“There is a world named Constant Renown, where a Tathāgata named Chief Beyond Hearing currently resides and preaches the Dharma.
These bodhisattvas have come from there to partake of your meal, desiring to hear and examine the false doubts harbored by the king.”

At that time, by the power of the aspirations established by the bodhisattvas and the original vows of the Tathāgata, the bowl flew naturally through the air and was cast into the Eight-Flavored Bathing Pond, where it was washed and purified.
The sons of good family, twenty-three thousand nāgas, and their consorts each took fragrances and placed them in the palms of the bodhisattvas.
When the king saw this, he was all the more filled with joy and stepped forward to prostrate himself before the youthful Mañjuśrī.
The youth Śrīmañjuśrī addressed the king, saying:
"You may prepare the offerings; you should know that now is the time.
The king immediately followed these instructions and set forth various kinds of food and exquisite, rare delicacies; the provisions were spread everywhere, yet they were never exhausted.
Thus, the five hundred meals originally provided by Ajātaśatru were made sufficient to satisfy all twenty-three thousand people, yet the food and drink remained as they were before.
King Ajātaśatru said to Mañjuśrī,
“Why is it that this meal remains as it was before and has not been digested?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Now, because you, O virtuous ones, have not yet fully exhausted your doubts, and because your doubts are not yet exhausted, this food remains undigested within you.
At that time, when the bodhisattvas had finished their meal, they immediately tossed their alms bowls into the air; the bowls remained suspended in the void, without any support, yet did not fall.
King Ajātaśatru asked Mañjuśrī,
"Where have all these bowls come to rest?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Just as the Great King harbors doubt, so too do these alms bowls remain therein.
Then the King replied,
"Do the bowls have no place to stand?"
Mañjuśrī replied:

“Just as the Great King’s doubts have no established basis, so too these bowls have no support and do not fall. All dharmas are likewise: they are entirely non-existent and have no place of abiding; for this reason, these dharmas also do not fall.”
