Chapter Ten: Resolving Doubts (Part Two). Chapter Ten: Resolving Doubts.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, seeing that the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas had finished eating and washed their hands, took a low seat and sat before Pūrṇa, wishing to hear the Dharma:
"I pray only that Pūrṇa will resolve my doubts."
Viśeṣamati replied,
"That which Your Majesty doubts cannot be resolved even by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. At that moment, the king,
realizing for himself that he was without rescue or protection, fell from his couch like a great tree severed at its base, collapsing and striking the ground.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"May Your Majesty be at ease; do not harbor fear or anxiety, nor be afraid. Why is this? Because—"
“Puṣya-matī, the Youthful One, is clad in the armor of great virtue; he has uttered these words through skillful means and expedient wisdom, so you may inquire at your leisure.
Thereupon, the King rose and asked Puṣya-matī:
“What did you say just now?”
"Could the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
not resolve my doubts for me? Pu-shou replied,
"What do you think, O King?"
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
engage in mental formations? He replied, "No."
Puśya asked again:
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, give rise to the thought of enlightenment and engage in practice?
He replied:
"No," he replied.
He asked again:
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, extinguish mental activities?"
He replied, "No. He asked again:
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, engage in conditioned phenomena? He replied, "No."
He asked again:
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, practice the unconditioned?
He replied:
"No. He asked again:
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the practice of the unconditioned?"
He replied, "No. Pu-shou spoke again:
"What do you think, O King?
Since all phenomena are without activity, and that which is without activity has no destination, can anyone truly teach or resolve the nature of these phenomena?"
He replied, “No.
“The King should understand this; it is for this reason that I have spoken these words.”
“The King’s doubts cannot be resolved even by the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, Great King!
Suppose there were someone who said to himself:
"If I were to pollute the void with dust, darkness, ashes, smoke, clouds, and mist,
would it be possible [to do so]? He replied:
"It cannot be defiled.
Pu-shou asked again:
"Suppose, Great King!"
"If I were to take this emptiness and wash it to make it clean,
would it be capable of such a task? He replied, "It could not."
Viśeṣamati replied: "It is so, Great King!
The body of the Tathāgata understands all phenomena to be like empty space; having attained supreme perfect enlightenment as one who is naturally pure, he is without any defilement."
For this reason, what dharma could there be that is defiled such that it would encounter opposition or limitation?
How could it possibly be definitively determined as something to be purified or removed?
Great King, contemplate the meaning of these dharmas; it is for this reason that I spoke as I did previously.
“Even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, cannot definitively resolve this.
“Furthermore, Great King, the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, do not attain an internal mind that has a place of abiding;”
One must not abide anywhere apart from the external mind. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are naturally pure and have no location; that which is naturally pure has no location, nor does it possess any aspiration or place of abiding.
Why is this? Because they have attained mastery, for all phenomena are naturally so.
Yet there is no "naturalness," for all phenomena have no arising or establishment.
There is no stumbling, for all phenomena are non-existent.
They are non-existent, for all phenomena are devoid of form and appearance.
They are devoid of form and appearance, for all phenomena are empty and void.
Truly unobstructed, for all phenomena lack the characteristic of instruction.
Truly beyond cultivation, for all phenomena are naturally non-existent.
Truly free from possession, for all phenomena are released and return to their source.
There is no place of refuge, for all phenomena are without separation.
There is no separation, for all phenomena are without arising.
There is nothing to rely upon, for all phenomena are naturally pure.
The nature of the mind is pure, for all phenomena are without differentiation, being equal to space.
It is peerless, for all phenomena have no companions or factions.
It is without a partner, for all phenomena are free from duality.
They are non-dual, for all phenomena are tranquil;
they are immeasurable, for all phenomena are without interruption;
they are boundless, for all phenomena have no limits.
How truly non-existent are all phenomena! For they abide by virtue of being inverted and lacking true reality.
How truly non-inverted are all phenomena! For they are eternally pure and have attained peace.
They are eternal, for all phenomena have no point of return.
They are pure, for all phenomena are fundamentally pure due to the clarity of realization.
They are spontaneously so, for all phenomena are selfless yet radiantly manifest.
How peaceful! For all phenomena are free from conceptualization.
How free from hesitation! For all phenomena are inwardly tranquil.
How free from deception! For all phenomena ultimately lack any fixed truth.
How tranquil and solitary are all phenomena, for they possess the characteristic of serenity!
How devoid of self are all phenomena, for they are free from the notion of "I"!
How free from outflows are all phenomena, for they possess the characteristic of liberation!
They have entered into tranquility, for all phenomena are free from conceptualization.
They are without fear, for all phenomena are free from diversity.
They have established the single equality, for all phenomena are equally governed by liberation.
How elusive are all phenomena, for they cannot be conceived as having a fundamental limit.
How thought-free are all phenomena, for they lack any basis for conceptualization and remain in silent stillness.
How they accord with emptiness, for all phenomena are free from all views.
They are without aspiration, for all phenomena are detached from the three periods of time.
They have severed the three periods of time, for all phenomena lack past, future, and present.
They are equal to the unconditioned, for all phenomena are ultimately unborn.
"What do you think, O King?
Those dharmas are unarisen and have not originated; they are non-existent and possess no ultimate truth.
How could anyone possibly defile them?"
He replied, “No. Pu-shou said:
"Can those dharmas be definitively resolved? He replied, "No."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said again:
"All dharmas are equal to nirvāṇa; it is because the Tathāgata understands this that he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
For this very reason, O King, your doubts cannot be resolved."
Therefore, Great King!

One must not practice that which involves contrivance or establishment; one must not follow a perverted mind. Rather, one should cultivate the contemplation of the True Dharma and contemplate the absence of an origin.
If one is able to examine this, then regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be understood; one does not dwell or associate with them.
If Your Majesty does not dwell or associate with any phenomena, this is what constitutes faith.
One who possesses such faith is one who is tranquil and still (*śānta*).
That which is tranquil is naturally pure;
that which is naturally pure involves no contriving.
That which involves no contriving means that all dharmas have no master; thus, one cultivates patience regarding all dharmas as having no creator.
Your Majesty should know this: that which is uncreated is *nirvāṇa*. When one reckons all phenomena (*dharmas*), they are likewise neither created nor destroyed;
there is neither creation nor non-creation—this is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Suppose, Great King!

One who is liberated in accordance with this is liberated through equality; because they are liberated through equality, regarding that Dharma there is no approaching and no reaching, neither increase nor decrease."
Why is this? Because among all phenomena there is no benefit or purpose, nor is there anything to be sought; all phenomena are without origin. That which is without origin is unarisen;
that which is unarisen is likewise without origin.
That which is without origin is equal and without distinction; therefore, it is said to be "without origin and without difference.
If Your Majesty understands and believes in this lack of origin, all doubts will naturally be severed.
"Furthermore, Great King!
The eye is neither defiled nor purified; because the intrinsic nature of the eye is without origin, that which is naturally without origin is called 'the eye'!"
The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise!
As for the mind, Great King, it is neither defiled nor purified;
because the natural state of the mind is without foundation, this lack of a foundational nature in its natural state is what is called "mind."
The King should understand this: form is neither defiled nor purified. Because form is naturally without origin, that which is naturally without origin is called "form."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise!

Consciousness is neither defiled nor purified; because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is without foundation, this lack of foundational nature in its intrinsic nature is what is called "consciousness."

Your Majesty should understand this: all dharmas are neither defiled nor purified. Because all dharmas are naturally without a fundamental basis, that which is naturally without a fundamental basis is called "all dharmas."
The mind has no form or color and cannot be seen; it is without harm, without location, and without verbal instruction.
It is like an illusion, abiding neither without nor within; the mind is fundamentally pure and naturally luminous.
If the mind is pure, there is neither defilement nor anything to be purified.

"Your Majesty should understand this: that fundamentally pure mind cannot be defiled; it is not something that can be purified, it is without falsehood, and it is without attachment or harm. Because of the absence of true conceptualization, one creates what is based on false conceptualization."
If there were any place of abiding, where ordinary, foolish beings cling to the defilements of desire—what could that possibly be?

Since there is no ultimate truth, they give rise to the notion of non-truth; because they lack truth, they do not produce the realization of truth. All phenomena abide in what is not the true truth, as they persist in that notion of non-truth.
It is like this, Great King:
for example, this space is without form and invisible, cannot be grasped, and there is nothing in it to be discarded nor any verbal instruction.
Suppose there were a person who said:

"Now this space is formless, invisible, and cannot be grasped; it is neither something to be discarded nor subject to verbal instruction. Yet, I now wish to defile this space with dust, smoke, flames, clouds, and mist."
The King replied, “I cannot. Puśya said:
"Thus it is, Great King!
The original purity of the mind is naturally luminous; it cannot be obscured, obstructed, or defiled by dust, smoke, flames, clouds, or mist."
For example, just as dust, smoke, flames, clouds, and mist abide in space, yet they never defile space or cause it to become impure;
so it is, Great King!

When the notion of a self arises and one claims "this is mine," and through the conditions of attachment one gives rise to lust, anger, and delusion, these do not defile the nature of the mind; the natural purity of the mind-phenomena remains undefiled.
Therefore, Great King!
You should harbor no doubts regarding this.

If you wish to know: the past mind and the future mind have no form or appearance; the future mind and the past mind likewise have no form or appearance; and the present mind has nothing upon which to rely and possesses nothing at all.

What the preceding mind contemplates does not obstruct what the succeeding mind contemplates, and what the succeeding mind contemplates does not obstruct what the preceding mind contemplates; the present mind is likewise so!
One clearly understands this and forms this contemplation: the mind has nothing that exists, yet it is not that nothing exists.

The past mind has already ceased; the future mind has not yet arrived; and the present has no abiding. Beholding all phenomena as having no abiding in the future, one eliminates all views without cause for wonder, for the sake of liberation.
Those with pure perception see that all phenomena are free from defilement, universally equal to the world and universally equal to clarity.
That which is unarisen has no verbal teaching; and being without verbal teaching, it does not abide anywhere.
Regarding the discourse on tranquility spoken by the World-Honored One, that which is tranquil, when reckoned according to those dharmas, has no location.
Suppose, Great King, there were someone who sought a location within the teachings and searched for all dharmas. Even so, Great King!
To abide in all dharmas without any conceptualization is to eliminate all knots of doubt, yet without there being anything among the dharmas to be decided upon or removed. Why is this so?
As for those who harbor doubts, they are equal to the Dharma itself without distinction; therefore, it is said that the Dharma-realm is governed by equality.
All dharmas and the Dharma-realm—within these dharmas, one should govern with equality.
Why is this? Because all phenomena enter the Dharma-realm;

if one is equal to the Dharma-realm, then one is equal to all phenomena. Therefore, it is called the equality of the Dharma-realm of all phenomena, for that Dharma-realm equally governs all phenomena.

When these words were spoken, King Ajātaśatru attained the patience of accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti); filled with joy and exultation, his heart attained great peace. He immediately joined his palms and exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Please speak these words to skillfully dispel my doubts.
Prabhāvyūha replied:
"Your Majesty should know that this constitutes a great, dark knot of doubt."
"Just as the King has ultimately explained all phenomena, he has uttered these words.
"Excellent, Mañjuśrī! You have spoken these words most skillfully, eloquently resolving our doubts."
The king replied again:
"Is it because one has extinguished all my aggregates and hindrances that, even if my life were to end and pass away, I would then reach the Way?"
Puṣya replied: "This is a profound doubt and obstruction for Your Majesty.

If you wish to ultimately realize all dharmas through extinction (nirvāṇa), how can you still harbor expectations regarding nirvāṇa? Having already realized that all dharmas are ultimate nirvāṇa, why do you still look forward to extinction?"
“Ultimate nirvana is that all dharmas are fundamentally pure and without arising.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru took a soft, exquisite robe worth hundreds of thousands and, holding it with his own hands, offered it to Puṣya to repay the kindness of the Dharma and to clothe his body.
Samantabhadra Kumārabhūta suddenly vanished; his body was no longer seen, nor could it be discerned where he had gone. A voice from the air said:
"Just as Your Majesty now does not behold the body of Samantabhadra, you should regard your own doubts in the same way!"
"Just as one views doubt, so too does one view all dharmas.
As one contemplates dharmas, what is seen is thus: seeing is non-seeing.
It was further said:
"Great King! Give the robe to the one you see as the Bodhisattva.
Next, to Prabhūtaratna, there sat a bodhisattva named Prajñāśrīdhvaja; King Ajātaśatru gave the robe to him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept the robe and spoke these words:
"I do not wish to be liberated from what exists, nor do I harbor resentment, nor do I seek parinirvāṇa."
I do not accept this robe by remaining close to the dharmas of ordinary persons;
nor do I receive it from those who have transcended the conduct of ordinary persons, nor from those still in training,
nor again from those who have transcended the dharmas of worldly dust.
It is not from those who have not yet entered the path of training, nor from those beyond training, that one receives this robe;
it is not from a pratyekabuddha, nor from one who has transcended the state of a pratyekabuddha, that one receives this robe.
I have not received [this teaching] from the Tathāgata, nor have I received it from anyone who has transcended the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
If, Great King, you were neither to practice this Dharma nor to abandon this Dharma, then it is from you that I would receive it.
Regarding those who are to receive and those who give, they are all equally one and the same, without distinction.
Such giving is that which has been taught by the Pure One, the Benefactor of the Multitudes.
King Ajātaśatru then placed his own garment upon the body of Prajñāśrīdhvaja; immediately, he vanished from his seat, and from the air there was again heard a voice saying:
"To him whose body has appeared, give this garment as an offering."
Next there was a bodhisattva named Śraddhānandapraśānta, to whom King Ajātaśatru offered a robe.
That bodhisattva said:
"I do not accept anything from the perspective of viewing my own body as having something received."
One does not receive anything from seeing others, nor from seeing attachment to defilements;
one does not receive anything from being free from defilements, nor from tranquil repose;
one does not receive anything from non-repose, nor from concentration of mind, nor from distracted intent, nor from wisdom, nor from the absence of wisdom.
The king then placed the garment upon the Bodhisattva, but it likewise did not appear; then, as if from the midst of the air, a voice spoke, saying:
"To one who manifests their body, give the garment."
Next there was a bodhisattva named Not Forsaking What Is Contemplated, to whom King Ajātaśatru offered a robe.
At that time, the bodhisattva likewise refused to accept it, saying these words:
"I do not receive anything by relying upon the body; [I receive] only from what is not relied upon."

They do not receive anything by relying on words, nor by relying on the mind, nor by relying on wisdom, nor by relying on meaning, nor by relying on the aggregates (*skandha*), nor by relying on the elements (*dhātu*), nor by relying on the sense-bases (*āyatana*), nor by relying on the truths (*satya*), nor by relying on the voice of the Buddha.
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are without reliance and without attachment; they are ultimately and eternally peaceful, and moreover, without agitation.
King Ajātaśatru then offered his robes to him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva likewise did not appear; however, a voice spoke from the air to the king, saying:
"To whichever Bodhisattva appears before you, give him the robe.
Next, the Bodhisattva named Zunzhi (Gaurī) sat down, and King Ajātaśatru gave him the robe.
At that time, the Bodhisattva also refused to accept it, saying these words:
"Your Majesty should know this: I do not accept anything from one who has escaped from lowliness."

If, Great King, you should give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, then because that mind is equal, the aspiration for the Way is equal; because the aspiration for the Way is equal, the Way is already equal, and thus the mind is also equal. Once the aspiration for the Way is equal, all dharmas are equal. One who is able to equalize all dharmas may then accept the robe. Regarding all dharmas, they neither accept nor reject them, nor do they grasp at anything. They are liberated from all dharmas, having neither intention nor non-intention. Beholding all dharmas, they see no self and do not conceive of a self. A practitioner who acts in this manner may then accept the robe.
King Ajātaśatru offered him his robes, but he immediately vanished.
Then a voice resounded from the air, saying:
"To whoever appears, give the robes."
Next, there was a bodhisattva named Samādhipuṣpārāja, to whom King Ajātaśatru offered his robe as a gift.
At that time, the bodhisattva likewise refused to accept it, saying these words:

"If the Great King practices all samādhis such that he harbors no attachments within the state of meditative concentration, and if he has faith and understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally pure, equal, and beyond liberation, then I shall accept this robe from him."
King Ajātaśatru placed the robe upon his body;
at that moment, the Bodhisattva likewise did not appear, for a voice was heard from the sky saying:
"Give the robe to him whose body is actually manifest."
Next, there sat a bodhisattva named Anuprāpta (Unattainable).
King Ajātaśatru offered him a robe, but that bodhisattva likewise refused to accept it, saying these words:

"If the Great King has attained faith in the crossing over all aggregates (*skandha*), and perceives that letters and sounds are entirely equal and ungraspable; if he has seen that all phenomena are unobtainable, and thus guides others toward the meaning of non-attainment; if he does not pursue worldly pleasures nor lead others toward ornamentation—if one acts in this way, I shall then receive from him."
King Ajātaśatru cast his robe at him.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva suddenly vanished; then, a voice arose from the sky, saying:
"Give the robe to him whose body is manifest."
Next, there was a bodhisattva named Viśuddhatrayamala (Pure from the Three Defilements), to whom King Ajātaśatru offered a robe.
At that time, the bodhisattva also refused to accept it, saying these words:
"If, Great King, you do not perceive a self-body and there is no recipient, and if the one who gives has no expectation—only if it is thus shall I accept the robe."
King Ajātaśatru cast his robe at him, but it likewise did not appear.
Then a voice arose in the air, saying:
"Give the robe to him whose body has appeared."
Next, the bodhisattva named Transformer of All Dharmas (Huà zhūfǎ wáng) sat down, and King Ajātaśatru offered him his robe.
At that time, the bodhisattva also refused to accept it, saying:
"Even if the Great King were to manifest as a śrāvaka and enter parinirvāṇa, he would not truly pass away."
He manifests as a pratyekabuddha and enters parinirvāṇa, yet he does not pass into extinction;
he manifests as a Tathāgata and enters parinirvāṇa, yet he does not pass into extinction.
There is no dharma of beginning or end, and no dharma of extinction; it is for this reason that I have accepted the robe.
King Ajātaśatru cast his robe at him, but it likewise did not appear.
A voice from the air said:
"Whoever manifests their body shall give the robe to him."
King Ajātaśatru offered robes in successive order, yet none of the bodhisattvas appeared;
each of them spoke, saying, "To whoever appears, give the robe."
The couches, beds, desks, and tables also vanished and were no longer visible.
King Ajātaśatru said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Those who are present now should receive these robes; you, O Benevolent One, are most honored and praised by the Buddha, and it is fitting that you accept them."
Mahākāśyapa said:
"I have not yet eradicated lust, anger, and delusion; therefore, my present body should not receive these robes.

I have not abandoned ignorance, nor removed the craving for desire, nor severed suffering and affliction, nor extinguished the formative tendencies (*saṃskāra*). I have not realized cessation, nor have I followed the path."

I have neither seen the Buddha nor heard the Dharma; I have not attended the assembly of the noble ones, nor have I relinquished worldly afflictions. I have neither produced mental conceptions nor abandoned them; I have neither established wisdom nor departed from it. My eyes are not pure, yet I do not construct wisdom, nor is there anything to be extinguished.
Those who give to me do not obtain great merit, nor is it that they have no merit at all.
I am neither within the dharmas of birth and death, nor am I in the dharma of extinction.
Those who give to me cannot exhaustively attain the virtue of manifold blessings.
"If the Great King can practice such protection of all beings as this, I shall accept these robes.
King Ajātaśatru cast the robes toward him, and he suddenly vanished from sight.
While he was in mid-air, a voice spoke, saying:
"Give your robes to those whose bodies appear.
King Ajātaśatru then bestowed robes one after another, yet each time they vanished from sight.
In this manner, all these great disciples, one by one, vanished in a state of bewilderment and were no longer seen; when all five hundred had gone, they again heard a voice say:
"Give the body that the King has beheld as an offering of clothing."
He then thought to himself:
"The Bodhisattva and the Śrāvakas have both vanished; I shall return to my primary queen.
He entered the palace and searched everywhere, yet he did not see any of the court ladies.

King Ajātaśatru then attained proximity to such a state of meditative concentration that, within his field of vision, he saw no forms; he saw neither men nor women, neither boys nor girls, neither the large nor the small, nor did he see walls, trees, houses, or city walls—continually perceiving only the perception of his own body.
Again, he heard a voice in the air saying, "Give the garment to him whose body appears.
The King immediately put it on himself; he no longer saw his own body, and immediately thereafter, all perceptions of form were cleared away like snow.
Again, a voice was heard saying:

"Suppose, Great King, you do not perceive the existence of any forms or images; if you view doubt with softness and tranquility, you should regard it as if you were seeing doubt itself. To view all phenomena is likewise thus."
That which is "seeing nothing" is itself seeing, for it is free from all views.
If one were to see anything while being free from views, then that would be "nothing seen," and one would not be free from views.

"One who sees in this way is able to practice equal contemplation (*samatā-darśana*). If one does not perceive anything among all phenomena, being without such perception constitutes equal contemplation.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru was entirely freed from all conceptualizations and attachments; arising from samādhi, he immediately returned and saw the assembly, the queens, the court ladies, the city walls, and the palaces, all exactly as they were before.
King Ajātaśatru addressed Puṣya said:
"Whence has this great assembly gathered?
Furthermore, why was it not seen by me while I was standing before it?"
Viśeṣamati replied,
"Just as the Great King’s doubts converge, so too do those in the assembly currently reside there.
He asked again:
“Great King!
Do you see this assembly?
He replied:
“I have seen it. Pu-shou asked:
“In what way have you seen it?”
"And yet they see with doubt; those who behold the assembly are likewise so!
He asked again:
"By what means do they see with doubt?"
He replied, "Just as those who attend the assembly see various forms and colors before their eyes, so too is doubt; it is neither seen internally nor externally.
He asked again:
“Great King!
The World-Honored One has said:
‘One who commits a heinous crime finds no place of rest and there is no interval [of respite]. Do you know for yourself that you shall go to hell?”
The King immediately replied:
"How is this, Puṣya?
When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, attained perfect enlightenment, did he perceive any dharma that returned to prison?"
“Does this lead to the three miserable realms? Does this lead to the heavens?
Does this lead to nirvāṇa? He replied, “No.”
"Great King!

Mañjuśrī perceives that I have now awakened to the realization of all dharmas; yet regarding the dharmas thus realized, even among all the teachings of the sūtras, nothing is to be apprehended. Whether one goes to hell, is born in the heavens, or enters parinirvāṇa—all dharmas are entirely suchness."
If one who contemplates emptiness were to differentiate the destination to which emptiness leads, there would be no going to hell, no reaching the heavens, and no returning to nirvāṇa.
All dharmas are indestructible;
all dharmas ultimately converge in the dharma-dhātu.
That which is the dharma-realm does not descend into the evil destinies, does not ascend to the heavens, and does not return to nirvāṇa.
That which is contrary to the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) is called the dharma-realm; the principle of all immediate transgressions is called the dharma-realm.

That which is fundamentally pure is called the immediate transgressions, and those immediate transgressions are called fundamental purity; therefore it is said that all dharmas are fundamentally pure.
Therefore, Puṣya!
All dharmas reach the state of non-arising; by this, one knows for oneself that there is no returning to the evil realms, nor ascending to heaven, nor entering nirvāṇa.
Puṣya replied: "In what way, Great King, do you disrupt the teachings of the Buddha?
He answered:
"I, too, do not contravene the instructions and commands of the World-Honored One, nor do I distort the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?

The World-Honored One has analytically expounded the limit of non-self and taught the source of the True Truth; since there is no self, there is likewise no person. Since the person does not exist, sentient beings are empty and void, and there is nothing substantial."
"Judging by this, there is nothing created, nor is there an agent, nor is there one who receives.
He asked again:
"Great King!"
"Has your doubt been severed?
He replied, "It has already been thoroughly investigated and eliminated!"
Puṣya asked: "O Great King,
have your doubts been severed?"
He replied,
“It is forever severed.
Pu-shou asked again:
"Now, why does Your Majesty, amidst this assembly, know that the king has committed a heinous crime yet say there is no such crime? He replied, "No."
He asked again,
"How so? He replied:
“Those who have already committed transgressions but are liberated from fetters and have attained realization;
those various transgressors are precisely those who encounter transgression.

Those various transgressions are the Bodhisattva’s patience in accordance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*), by which they cause all people to enter this patience; one should not grasp at or cling to those transgressions.”
"Samantabhadra!
What is called 'rebellion'—from that [state] to this, there are no rebellions whatsoever. For this reason, one should not conceptually grasp at rebellions therein."
Then the Bodhisattva Prajñāśrīdhvaja raised his voice and praised him, saying:
"It is because you have adorned and cleared the path of the Great King that you are now able to attain such a dharma-patience."
The King then replied:
“All dharmas are fundamentally and ultimately pure;
furthermore, all dharmas are ultimately tranquil and silent, free from any defilement.”
For this reason, it cannot be defiled or made impure; it is the Way of non-attachment, and this is what is called the Way.

Furthermore, that Way does not return to birth and death, nor does it reach nirvana. Among the paths of the various worthies and sages, there is no one who governs the Way; there is no arising of the Way, and this is what is called the Way. In the Way, there is no "Way."
When King Ajātaśatru spoke these words, he attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma that accords with the truth (anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti) through clear insight.

At that time, forty-two women of the inner palace, having witnessed the majestic power and miraculous transformations of Mañjuśrī, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Five hundred commoners became free from dust and defilement, and their Dharma-eye was purified.
At that time, an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of people gathered at the gate of the royal palace, desiring to hear the Dharma and to offer worship and service.
The youth Prabhūtaratna pressed down upon this earth with his toes.

At that time, the city of Rājagṛha was entirely made of lapis lazuli; all the inhabitants dwelling within the city saw Prabhūtaratna, the Bodhisattvas, and the Śrāvakas, just as one sees the reflection of one’s own face in a clear mirror.

The Youthful Samantabhadra preached the Dharma to those who had gathered according to their individual needs; eighty-four thousand people who heard the sutra attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and five hundred people all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

11. Chapter on the Innate Purity of the Mind (Part II). Chapter Eleven: On the Innate Purity of the Mind. At that time, Puṣya addressed King Ajātaśatru, his retinue, and the countless other beings who had gathered, instructing and transforming them by preaching the Dharma.

He immediately rose from his seat and, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, King Ajātaśatru, his ministers and officials, and countless other people, departed from the palace gate and proceeded along the road.
On the road, he saw a man who had killed his own mother and was staying beneath another tree, weeping in anguish and crying out, "Alas!
How can this person be brought to ultimate deliverance in the present life?"

He reproached himself, saying, "What I have done is monstrous; by committing such a great transgression, I have endangered my own mother and shall surely fall into hell. Nevertheless, that person should still cultivate the practice of the Vinaya.

At that time, Samantabhadra manifested a transformation-body before the assembly of bhikṣus; he immediately went to where the woman who had killed her mother was, and stopping midway at no great distance from her, he remained there.
The one who had harmed his mother saw from afar his parents traveling together with their son.
The parents asked the son, "Is this the correct path? The son replied:
"This is not the correct path," they said,
as they alternately gave rise to disputes.
Thereupon, the emanated son manifested anger and killed his emanated parents.

The son of the one who had committed the heinous crime saw from afar that the transformed son was harming the transformed parents; overcome by bitter grief and unable to restrain himself, he immediately went to the place where the mother-harmer was and said to him:
"If I kill my parents, I shall surely fall into hell."
Weeping, he said:
"What can be done? What plan should be devised?
Then the one who had killed his mother thought to himself:
"This person who has come here has harmed both his parents; I have only endangered my mother, yet that man's folly and sin are beyond measure!
My own act of rebellion is still less grave than his, and even the punishment he receives would seem light to me."
Those emanated beings were filled with profound and bitter sorrow, and they proclaimed in unison:
"We shall go to the abode of the Buddha Śākyamuni; for those who have no savior, the Buddha shall provide salvation;
for those who are terrified, he shall comfort them and remove their afflictions. We shall follow and uphold that which the Buddha has taught us."
At that time, the emanated person wept as he proceeded along the road, walking ahead; the one who had killed his mother followed closely behind him, thinking:
"Just as he repents, so shall I do!"
"My offense is slight, while that person's is extremely grave.
The transformed person went to the Buddha, prostrated himself on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!"
"I have committed a great rebellion by harming my two parents; how could I have incurred such a grave offense?
The Buddha told the transformed person:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Acting with utmost sincerity and without deception, ensuring that your words and deeds accord with one another, you should approach the Tathāgata and speak words of truth, refraining from double-tongued speech and not disparaging yourself.
One should personally reflect upon and examine the method of observing the mind: by means of which mind do you endanger your two parents—
is it the past mind,
or the future mind?
Is it the present mind?
That past mind has already ceased and perished;
that present mind has already departed, having no location and no direction, and being unknown as to where it dwells.
The future mind has likewise not yet arrived; it has no place of accumulation, is not seen to return, and has no coming or going.
You should know this: the mind does not abide within the body, nor does it come from without; it has no objective realm, it does not dwell between the two, and it cannot be found in the interim.
When one examines the mind, it likewise possesses no five colors—blue, red, yellow, white, or black.
You should understand this!
The mind is colorless, invisible, has no dwelling place, and does not undergo retrogression.
There is no verbal teaching and it cannot be grasped; it is just like an illusion.
If you, my son, wish to examine the mind, it cannot be differentiated and cannot be comprehended.
One cannot name it as lust, one cannot fathom it as anger, and one cannot know it as delusion; there is no lust, anger, or delusion.
Son, you should understand that the mind has no activity of birth and death, nor does it have anything produced, nor does it have anything manifested, nor does it appear in the present.
The mind is pure, yet it is neither defiled nor is there one who purifies it.
The mind is not here, nor is it there; it does not abide in another place. It is like empty space: it has no equal, no form or image, and no verbal teaching.

The wise person should not rely upon anything; do not say "I," nor claim "this is mine. Do not create a dwelling place, do not form conceptualizations, do not create an ultimate state, and do not engage in purposeful action. Do not speak of one's own body, do not say "I" or "self," and do not dwell on the past.
Why is this so? You should know, my son!
All phenomena are entirely without abiding, just like empty space.
My son, listen to this!

One who understands in this way, the Buddha does not say that person has escaped from the dharmas; if one is defiled, one does not fail to return to the evil realms, but if the mind is pure and free from defilement, then there are no realms of existence.
At that time, the manifested person immediately exclaimed:
"How unprecedented! O God among Gods!

The Tathāgata, by means of which he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment, has fully realized the Dharma-realm: there is no agent, nor is there any recipient; there is no one who is born, nor anyone who enters parinirvāṇa; there is nothing upon which to rely."
"I wish to leave the household life; through the Buddha, the World-Honored One, may I become a śramaṇa and receive full ordination.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
At that time, the transformed person appeared before him as a śramaṇa and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
Having attained supernormal powers, I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, that transformed person rose forty-nine chi above the ground and entered parinirvāṇa in mid-air; fire issued from his body and consumed it.
At that time, the rebellious son saw that transformed person had become a śramaṇa, heard and received the Dharma, and listened to what the Buddha had spoken.
He thought to himself:
"Previously, that man endangered his own parents, yet before the World-Honored One he became a śramaṇa and immediately attained parinirvāṇa."
"Now, for what reason should I not emulate that man and become a śramaṇa, so as to likewise attain parinirvāṇa?
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I too have committed a heinous crime by endangering my mother's life."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!

You are most sincere and without deceit; your words and deeds correspond with one another. Having come before the Tathāgata, you have spoken words of truth, neither engaging in double-tongued speech nor harming yourself."
One should personally reflect upon and observe the method of examining the mind: by means of which mind does one endanger one's parents—
by the past mind or the future mind?
Is it the present mind?
That past mind has already ceased and perished;
that present mind has already departed elsewhere, having no location and no direction, and its whereabouts are unknown.
The future mind has likewise not yet arrived; it has no place of accumulation, its return is not seen, and it neither comes nor goes.
You should know this!
The mind does not abide within the body, nor does it come from without, nor does it have an objective realm; it does not dwell between the two, nor can it be found in the interim.
When one examines its mind, it likewise possesses no five colors—blue, red, yellow, white, or black.
You should understand this!
The mind is colorless; it cannot be seen, nor does it have any abode. It does not regress, it has no verbal instruction, it cannot be grasped, and it is like an illusion.
If you wish to examine the mind, it cannot be differentiated, it cannot be comprehended, and it cannot be named as lust, nor investigated as anger, nor known as delusion.
Free from lust, anger, and delusion, my son, you should know that while moving within the cycle of birth and death, there is nothing done, nothing manifested, and nothing appearing before one.
The mind is pure, yet it is neither defiled nor is there one who purifies it.
The mind is not here, nor is it there; it is not in any other place. It is like empty space: it has no equal, no form or appearance, and no verbal expression.

One who possesses clear knowledge should not rely upon anything; do not say "I," nor claim "this is mine. Do not create a dwelling place, do not form conceptualizations, and do not establish an ultimate state. Do not act for the sake of anything, do not speak of one's own body, do not say "I" or "self," and do not dwell on the past.
Why is this so? You should know, my son!
All phenomena are entirely without abiding, just like empty space.
My son, listen to this!

One who understands in this way, the Buddha does not say, is liberated from dharmas; if one is defiled, one does not fail to return to the evil destinies, but if the mind is pure and free from defilement, then there are no destinies at all.
At that time, the fires of hell emerged from the pores of the person who had committed the offense; the pain was extremely severe and there was no protection. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am now being burned; O God among Gods, grant me relief! I take refuge in the Great Sage."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm and placed it upon the crown of the man’s head; the fire was immediately extinguished and his suffering ceased.

Beholding the various marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s body, his physical pain subsided and he attained peace. He then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying, “I wish to become a śramaṇa.”
The Buddha immediately granted his permission, and he became a śramaṇa at once.

Then the World-Honored One preached the Four Noble Truths for him; upon hearing them, the man was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye. He practiced the teachings of the Dharma and attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, eventually realizing and attaining the state of an arhat.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa.
The World-Honored One replied:
"According to your wish.

At that time, the bhikṣu leaped into the air to a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground; from his body he emitted fire that consumed his own form, while hundreds of thousands of devas and humans came through the air to make offerings.
At that time, Śāriputra saw that person receive this teaching of the precepts and attain nirvāṇa; he was struck with wonder and amazement, and approaching the Buddha, he said:
"Truly, this is beyond reach."
O God among Gods!

The Dharma and Vinaya taught through the Tathāgata’s grace enable even those who act in opposition to receive his instruction; yet such practitioners differ in their capacities, and only the Tathāgata is capable of saving them!

Samantabhadra the Youthful, clad in the armor of great virtue, is able to perceive the fundamental dispositions of all sentient beings and deliver them accordingly; this is a realm not within the reach of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Śāriputra."
It is exactly as you have said; this is the realm of the Great Being, the Bodhisattva of Dharma-patience.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What you perceive as falling into hell, the Buddha beholds as the dharma of ultimate extinction (nirvāṇa).
When you perceive someone who should have attained parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One, through his profound knowledge, sees that such a person has instead fallen into the evil realms.

Or, when there is a man of virtue who, being content, dwells in seclusion, upholds the precepts, and abides in samādhi, you consider him to have reached the state of parinirvāṇa; yet the Tathāgata perceives that such a person will, on the contrary, fall into hell.

Why is this? Beings such as yourselves are detached from mental activity and cannot universally examine the source of the minds of sentient beings; the conduct of the multitudes of living beings is inconceivable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Do you see this man who killed his mother?
Having heard the exposition of the profound Dharma, has he attained parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder?
He replied, "I have seen them,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"This woman who killed her mother has planted the roots of many virtues under five hundred buddhas; she has heard the profound and wondrous Dharma, through which she has understood that the fundamental nature of the mind is pure and radiant.
Furthermore, because this person has entered this scripture, she has received all dharmas and attained liberation."
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! For this reason,
if sons of good family or daughters of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to hear the meaning of this Dharma and immediately believe and rejoice in it;”

Furthermore, regarding those who are deluded and whose minds are estranged, yet who follow evil companions and commit transgressions without losing their patience for the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and who eventually attain liberation in the realm of no-remainder (anupadhiśeṣa)—I do not say that such individuals fall into the evil destinies.
The merit obtained by one who possesses faith and delight in such profound and wondrous teachings is indeed like this!

For this reason, if those of such a kind abide upon the right path and, upon hearing this scripture, immediately believe and delight in it, expounding its impartial verses and stanzas, and extensively analyzing and explaining them for others, their virtue shall be exactly as described!
"How much more so for those who practice and cultivate according to what has been taught?

Then Prajñākūṭa, together with the various bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Kāśyapa, King Ajātaśatru, and countless others, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet in homage, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that Prabhūtaratna and all those in the assembly were seated, addressed King Ajātaśatru: "Great King,
has your doubt been severed?"
He replied: "Indeed so,
O worthy one!"
"It will be severed upon investigation.
He asked again:
"How is it severed?"
He replied:

"Neither accepting nor rejecting—this is called 'severance. Furthermore, when there is nothing to be attained, and one has forever and completely understood both the beginning and the end such that no defilement exists, that is severance!"
Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One, how much of King Ajātaśatru’s task has been completed, and how much remains?
The World-Honored One replied:

"The King's remaining karmic retribution is like a mustard seed, while the sins he has extinguished are like Mount Sumeru; he has entered the profound Dharma and attained the meaning of the sutras taught therein, reaching the state of non-arising."
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Will King Ajātaśatru go back to the evil realms?
The Buddha replied:
"Just as a son of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, while in a multi-storied pavilion of seven treasures adorned with lattices, descends to Jambudvīpa and immediately returns to his original place;
so it is, Śāriputra!"
The hell into which King Ajātaśatru entered was named Piṇḍila (translated into Chinese as Jiyù,
"Accumulation of Desires").
Upon entering it, he immediately emerged, and his body did not suffer the affliction of pain.
Śāriputra said: “It is difficult to fathom,
World-Honored One!”
Is King Ajātaśatru’s spiritual faculties so clear and penetrating?
And how is it that he can thus eliminate such various transgressions and such heavy calamities—the poison of the hells?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"King Ajātaśatru has previously made offerings to seventy-two billion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, planting many roots of virtue and receiving all the scriptures. Regarding the Dharma he has heard, he encourages others toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Do you not see Pūrṇa?"
He replied, “I have seen them.
The World-Honored One said:

“Samantabhadra Kumārabhūta exhorted Ajātaśatru to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Throughout incalculable kalpas, there were the Tathāgata Vimalagarbha and countless other Buddhas; within those kalpas, there were three hundred million perfectly awakened ones, all of whom were exhorted by Samantabhadra to turn the wheel of Dharma and remain for a long life, something that even a hundred thousand World-Honored Ones could not have accomplished.”
When King Ajātaśatru seeks to resolve his doubts through the teaching of the Dharma, it is only Samantabhadra who can sever the net of his doubts for this king. Why is this?
Because the youth Samantabhadra has frequently heard this profound Dharma from various Buddhas; therefore, one should form this understanding.

As for those bodhisattvas who are to be delivered, they must first follow their original resolve to find their fundamental teacher; only then, through the teaching of the Dharma for them, can they attain understanding!

King Ajātaśatru has emerged from the Saṃjīva Hell with the intent to disparage it, and he has been reborn in a world above this one, five hundred buddha-fields away. That world is called Adorned (Vyūha), and its Buddha is named Ratnaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma there.
When you behold Puṣya again and hear the profound sūtras in that land, you shall immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When Maitreya Bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment, you shall descend once more to this Sahā world-system, where you shall be known as the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Acalo!
Tathāgata Maitreya shall proclaim for this assembly the deeds previously performed by Bodhisattva Acalā, and furthermore, he shall analyze and expound the ultimate meaning of this sutra.

"The Great Being Acala was once a great king of the world during the time of the Buddha Śākyamuni, named Ajātaśatru. Following the words of evil friends, he murdered his own father; however, upon hearing the sūtras preached by Mañjuśrī, he attained the Dharma-patience of Accordance (Anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti), whereby his transgressions were eliminated so that none remained."

When the Tathāgata Maitreya preached this Dharma of the sutra for the sake of Bodhisattva Acalamati, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas eliminated immeasurable, incalculable accumulations of sinful transgressions.
"In this way, Śāriputra,
from now on for eight hundred incalculable eons, King Ajātaśatru shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices, transform sentient beings, and adorn and purify Buddha-fields."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Those beings transformed by King Ajātaśatru—whether they are on the stage of a śrāvaka, the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or practicing the Mahāyāna—all such beings shall have their veils of sin [cleansed], be free from the defilement of dust and grime, and have all doubts eliminated so that no hesitation remains.
After more than eight thousand incalculable kalpas, he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One.

The kalpa shall be named *Priyadarśana*, the world shall be called *Anabhinirvṛttaskandha*, and the Buddha’s name shall be *Viśuddhaviṣaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha*, with a lifespan of fourteen kalpas.
There was a great assembly of seven hundred thousand śrāvakas, all of whom possessed wisdom and understanding and were resolved upon the eight gates of liberation;
there were also twelve billion bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained the perfection of wisdom and skillful means.
After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for one hundred million years.
All the sentient beings in the world-system of Akaniṣṭha who reach the end of their lives without harboring doubt will, after their final passing, not fall into the three miserable realms.
If the Tathāgata Viśuddhaviṣaya were to preach the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings, they would all be rid of every defilement; free from worldly afflictions, they would all attain purity.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

When people meet one another, they must not judge each other’s characteristics. The reason why one should not judge others’ characteristics is that the faculties of human beings are difficult to perceive; only the Tathāgata can judge the characteristics of others, and those whose conduct is like that of a Buddha may likewise judge the characteristics of others.
The worthy Śāriputra and the great assembly were filled with wonder and leaped for joy, saying these words:
"From this day forward, for as long as our lives shall last, we will no longer look to others, nor dare we say of anyone: 'Such a person goes to hell,' or 'Such a person shall attain parinirvāṇa.'"
"Why is this? Because the conduct of sentient beings is inconceivable.

At that time, as the Buddha spoke this parable to resolve the doubts of Ajātaśatru, thirty-two thousand devaputras conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, each making a vow, saying:
"When the World-Honored One Śuddhalokadhātu attains perfect enlightenment, we shall be born in that Buddha-land and not create a world of desire.
The Buddha then prophesied that they would indeed be born in that land.

Chapter Twelve: The Prediction for Candraprabha (Part Two) King Ajātaśatru had a crown prince named Candraprabha, who was eight years old. He untied the jeweled necklace from his neck, scattered it over the Buddha, and said:

"By this merit, may I assist in the unsurpassed, right, and true path. By this root of goodness, when the Tathāgata Viśuddhaviṣaya attains perfect enlightenment, I vow to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King and sovereign of the four quarters in that land!"
For as long as their life lasts, they shall make offerings to the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they shall uphold his relics and receive the sūtras, and thereafter they shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become the Most Perfectly Awakened One!

These scattered pearl necklaces then formed in mid-air a pavilion of seven precious gems with latticed windows, with four pillars on each side, equal in height above and below, solemn, upright, and exquisitely beautiful. Within that pavilion were placed four jeweled couches spread with celestial silks; the Tathāgata sat upon them, adorned with his marks and signs of excellence.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.

According to the nature of the World-Honored One’s smile, countless, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth, illuminating inconceivable and boundless worlds of the Buddhas. They surpassed the palaces of Brahmā and Māra; the radiance of the sun and moon was naturally eclipsed, and the beams circled his body for innumerable turns before entering through the crown of his head.
The worthy Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and praised him in verse:
"Transcending all wisdom, Surpassing all hindrances;
He understands the various classes of sentient beings, And the fundamental source of their mental activities."
Discerning the beginning and the end, you preach the Dharma according to the occasion;
O World-Illuminator, please explain: for what reason do you smile with joy?
Sentient beings throughout the ten directions stand before you in every place.
Countless billions of trillions of beings, each one posing difficult questions,
are able to have their doubts resolved by the Holy Teacher, the Sage of Benevolence.
Excellent! I pray you explain: out of compassion, why do you rejoice?
Those past Buddhas were established in the most supreme state.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, in future ages,
like the sands of the Ganges River,
you will discern and know the six realms of existence, crossing over to the ultimate shore through wisdom.
Therefore, he manifests a joyful smile, purifying defilements and resolving doubts.
His radiance surpasses that of the sun and moon, eclipsing the palaces of Māra, Śakra, and Brahmā;
it penetrates through all the Cakravāḍa mountains and shines beyond the peaks of every mountain range.
"You have brought peace and security to the common people and exhausted all their hardships;
you have skillfully taught to remove all defilements. For what reason, then, do you smile with such joyful delight?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Have you seen Prince Candraprabha? He replied, “Indeed, I have.”
The Buddha said:
“Candraprabha!

By planting these roots of merit before the Buddha, you have thereby encouraged and assisted the path toward unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; you shall gradually and progressively accumulate [merit] as you cultivate the bodhisattva practices.”

When the Tathāgata Viśuddhaviṣaya attains the path of Buddhahood, this prince shall be born in that Buddha-field as a Wheel-Turning King, making offerings and serving the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Viśuddhaviṣaya, providing for his needs until the end of his life.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he shall make offerings to the relics and uphold the True Dharma; when the Dharma has completely vanished, he shall pass away and be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. There, in that kalpa, he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One, known by the name Candraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One!
"The lifespan of the Buddhas in all those lands, as well as the assemblies of bhikṣus, shall be exactly like that of the World-Honored One in this Pure Realm, without any difference.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from other worlds to this Sahā world together with Mañjuśrī, having heard these words, came forward and addressed the Buddha:

"Wherever the youthful Mañjuśrī travels, one should observe that the lands he visits are entirely filled by Tathāgatas, leaving no vacancy; thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, need no longer exert themselves in concern."
Why is this so? Indeed, World-Honored One!

That which is encompassed by Mañjuśrī shall never have any miserable realms, nor any lack of leisure, nor any demonic activities, karmic obstructions, or defilements. In whatever regions, provinces, districts, towns, villages, or walled cities this true scripture is circulated, one shall behold that place as a dwelling where the Tathāgata resides, leaving no empty space.
The World-Honored One said: "So it is, so it is!
Son of good family!"
Just as you have said, wherever this sutra is proclaimed, that is where the Tathāgata dwells, and that is where the Tathāgata earnestly bestows his teachings.
Furthermore, son of good family!

In the distant past, at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I received my prediction of enlightenment in that world. Upon the ground where I had spread my hair, Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata stepped across my hair and scattered lotus flowers over it; thereupon I attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and he bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"After incalculable kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata!"
"Thus it was, noble son!
At that time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
'None of you shall step upon this ground.'"

Why is this? This place shall become a divine temple and a Buddha-stūpa for the heavens and the world; since the Bodhisattva spread his hair upon this spot, one who attains the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) may wish to erect a stūpa here. Who would not desire to do so?
Those eighty billion devaputras simultaneously cried out:
"We shall arise!
At that time, there was an elder in the assembly named Bhadradatta who addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I shall erect a stupa and a monastery on this site.
The Buddha said, "You may do so."
"O son of noble family!
At that very spot, the elder Bhadradatta erected a stūpa made of the seven treasures, complete with all its adornments. He then returned to Dīpaṃkara and asked the Buddha:
'I have raised a stūpa of the seven treasures at that location; where does this merit lead? "
Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata then replied to him, saying:

"If the Elder wishes to know: suppose a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If one were to take all the soil and dust from the ground beneath his feet down to the very limits of the earth—each particle as large as a *śarīra* relic—and offer it in worship, and furthermore, were to fill the space up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven with the seven treasures and give them as alms to the Buddha; [the merit of the former would still surpass that of the latter]."

If one were to compare it with the merit of building stūpas and temples, the latter would ultimately not equal it; the merit of stūpas and temples is so vast that it is difficult to calculate. The root of virtue planted by the elder here shall, as I now bestow this prediction upon the māṇava, lead him to the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
"If you attain Buddhahood, I shall likewise establish you in the definitive path of the Great Way.
"Noble son, what do you think?
At that time, was the elder named Bhadradatta anyone else?"
"Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
Within this assembly there is a son of a householder named Śreṇika!

I now bestow upon him the prediction that in a future age he shall attain the Way of the Buddha, being known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One!"
For this reason, sons of good family, daughters of good family, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās!

Whether standing or sitting, if you write down this sutra, uphold, recite, read, and explain it to others, then from that place down to the very limits of the earth, all the dust shall become sentient beings; furthermore, this entire land shall be like śarīras.
Why is this so? It is because a Bodhisattva who has attained forbearance (*kṣānti*) likewise accomplishes all such virtues!

Therefore, the Buddha earnestly entrusts this to you: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them as alms to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—doing so three times each day and night without indolence, offering at the proper times for the duration of an eon or even more—an act such as this would not equal the merit of receiving this sūtra.

King Ajātaśatru, having eliminated all doubts and being free from hesitation, purified the aggregates (*skandha*) and the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and discerned the equality of all phenomena (*dharma*). Whether writing, reading, receiving, upholding, or reciting them, or hearing them with faith and joy, one should record them on bamboo or silk, and treat these scrolls with reverence and care, so that this True Dharma may endure for a long time. The merit and blessings of this far exceed those previously mentioned; they are immeasurable and beyond limit.
The Buddha said,

“Noble son! If one upholds the prohibitions and precepts for a hundred kalpas and universally understands contentment, only then can one dwell in seclusion with a joyful resolve that is never abandoned.”
Those who hear this sutra and believe in it with joy shall possess merit and blessings that surpass those who strictly observe the prohibitions and precepts.
Even if one were to practice patience for a hundred kalpas, enduring all the insults, verbal abuse, beatings, and the infliction of painful blows from all sentient beings,
yet if another person were to hear the essentials of this sutra and believe in it with joy, their merit and blessings would immediately transcend those of the former practitioner of patience.

If one were to practice diligence for a hundred kalpas, making offerings to all classes of sentient beings while having no attachment to one's own body or life, it would not equal the merit of one who hears this sutra and receives it with joy and faith.

If one were to practice meditative concentration for a hundred kalpas and remain undisturbed even when encountering provocations, it would not equal the merit of one who hears this sutra and receives it with joy and faith.

If one were to practice wisdom for a hundred kalpas, comprehensively grasping and understanding all things without exception, yet were to hear this chapter of the sutra on the ultimate, primordial purity and the natural clarity of mind, and then receive it with joy and faith, uphold the precepts, and recite it, the merit and blessings of such a person would far surpass the former, and they would be able to swiftly establish themselves in the various supernormal knowledges and perfect wisdom!
Then all the bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We have already received this sutra; wherever we travel among the various buddha-lands, we shall proclaim it in every place where we dwell.”
"Why is this? It is because the various sūtras perform the work of the Buddha.
At that time, the bodhisattvas raised their voices in praise and again scattered flowers throughout the trichiliocosm, saying these words:

“If this sutra is established and remains for a long time throughout Jambudvīpa, and the True Dharma of the World-Honored One, the Able One (Śākyamuni), is made manifest, then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta shall cause it to endure forever; for such a sutra as this, we have never before examined or heard.”
Even if we were to hear it, we would be unable to repay the Buddha’s kindness or that of Viśeṣacintin; by what means, then, should we perform a great offering?
O son of good family!
The kindness of one from whom one hears this sutra is difficult to repay.
If there is anyone who wishes to see the Tathāgata, they should regard such a person as they would the World-Honored One upon hearing this sutra.
If one wishes to make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, one should instead make offerings to this son of good family!
If you see a son or daughter of good family, you should regard them as the Buddha, the World-Honored One!

When the bodhisattvas had finished their praises, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and suddenly vanished from this buddha-field. Each returned to his own original land and remained before his respective Tathāgata, extensively expounding for others the Dharma as it had been received. Thus, before each of those Buddhas in their respective lands, they guided and transformed countless beings, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
13. Chapter on Entrustment (Part Two). Chapter Thirteen: On Entrustment. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying:

"Virtuous one, you should receive this sublime scripture of the True Dharma and explain it in detail for immeasurable people. It shall bring great peace and comfort, and great compassion; all devas and worldlings shall surely receive its grace."
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

Having already received the teaching of this sutra, I have likewise received and been initiated into this scripture by the Tathāgatas of the past; now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, I hear this Dharma.”
"So be it, Great Sage!
While the Tathāgata is present, I shall expound this sutra so that it may flow everywhere;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, while in Tuṣita Heaven, I shall explain this for the sake of all living beings, planting the roots of manifold virtues."
If there are sons or daughters of good family who,
in future ages, hear this sutra and resolve their minds upon the Mahāyāna, you should know that this is established by Maitreya.

If any malevolent Māras should seek an opportunity while one upholds this sutra, we shall, in accordance with the holy intent of the World-Honored One, protect them so that they remain free from flaw or deficiency.
The Buddha told Śakra:
“You should receive this sūtra, the ‘Chapter on Ajātaśatru,’ which severs all fetters. Why is this so?
If the devas and asuras should harbor resentment and engage in battle, they should recollect this sutra; then the devas will be victorious and the asuras will be subdued.
The Buddha said:
"Kauśika! I now entrust this to you:

wherever this sutra may be—whether in provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, cities, or villages—you must protect that land, so that enemies, adversaries, and those with grudges shall find no opportunity there."

Whether encountering government officials, being among bandits, meeting wild beasts, encountering spirits or ghosts, meeting thieves and robbers, or suffering the terrors of water or fire disasters, one should immediately contemplate this scripture and recite its verses;
thus, no enemies, rebels, or evil marauders shall be able to find an opportunity against them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Receive this sutra, uphold it, and recite it. Why is this so?

If there should be someone who seeks this essential sūtra from you, that son or daughter of good family will sever all doubts and be free from hesitation; they will wash away and forever eliminate all fetters, such that the veils of sin and the obstacles of Māra cannot obscure them, and their past calamities, malevolent harms, and hindrances will naturally vanish.
"Why is this? Because if one hears this sutra, there will be no further doubt.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"We have burdened you with our earnest exhortations and instructions; if those who commit rebellious acts enter into this essential scripture and rejoice with gladness, they shall be free from rebellion, free from harm, and free from the veil of transgression."
The elder Kāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, Great Sage! I bear witness to this sutra.

Previously, when we went to King Ajātaśatru’s palace to distinguish the nature of parricide, King Ajātaśatru immediately attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and the net of his doubts was instantly removed."
At that time, I thought to myself:
"Ajātaśatru originally did not understand all dharmas, nor did he distinguish between the various acts of parricide.
Indeed, World-Honored One!

All dharmas are fundamentally pure by their very nature; yet, one instead engages in conceptualization and calculation, positing a self and establishing various views, thereby failing to cultivate and refine the fundamental purity of all conflicting phenomena.
Just as Ajātaśatru, by associating with perversions and false conceptualizations, has brought about the affliction of diligent suffering;
if one thoroughly investigates this, then there will be no such difficulties.

From this day forward, I declare that all sentient beings are likewise without sin and without the laws of the evil realms; those who enter into this shall transcend and depart, free from beginning or end.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!”
"It is exactly as you have said; the governance of the path and its meaning by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is free from all defilement.
The Venerable Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!"
"Establish this sutra so that it may circulate throughout Jambudvīpa in the future final age.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from his left and right flanks, which universally illuminated the trichiliocosm. From the trees and the walls, there naturally issued forth these sounds:

"Once the Tathāgata has established this sutra, even if this sutra should be within the great ocean or during the time of the kalpa-ending conflagration, one must hear this scripture; it shall not be interrupted such that it cannot be heard."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Just as sounds emerge from trees and walls, it is truly as you have said: these virtuous men who have planted the roots of manifold merits shall never lose this sutra midway when they receive it in their final age."

When the Buddha preached this sutra, ninety-six thousand devas and humans were cleansed of dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; sixty-eight thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; twenty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising dharmas; eight thousand people were freed from all greed and desire; and the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system shook in six ways.
At that moment, a great sound universally proclaimed throughout the heavens and the world:
"All come to make offerings to this sutra!
The musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, universally proclaiming throughout the heavens and the world:
"All come to scatter flowers, burn incense, various perfumes, powdered incense, and unguents, and every face encounters this turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

The sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata here are all for the purpose of subduing the various heterodox paths, repelling all deviant practices, and suppressing the hosts of Māras; this is the seal of the Tathāgata, which constitutes the refined cultivation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma."
"O sons of noble family!
You should now discern and seek this Dharma-seal of ultimate right view.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, King Ajātaśatru, the youth Mañjuśrī, the Mahāsattva Maitreya, all the bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Ānanda, and others—as well as the devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha had said, were all filled with joy.
